en: May there be prosperity!
The Treatise of the Seventy Golden Verses. First Section.
Because of the affliction by the threefold suffering, there arises a desire to know the means for its removal.
If it is argued that this [desire] is useless since a remedy is seen in the world, we say no, because such remedies are neither certain nor final. (1)

The introduction to this noble work is stated as follows: Long ago, it is said, there was a great sage named Kapila, born from space (the son of Brahmā), whose nature consisted of the fourfold qualities of innate dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty. Beholding this world sinking in blinding darkness, great compassion arose within him, [thinking]: "Alas! This world indeed exists in blinding darkness. While reflecting thus upon the world, he saw a certain Brāhmaṇa of the Āsuri lineage who had performed sacrifices for a thousand years.

The self-concealed Ananta approached him and spoke these words: "O Āsuri, do you take delight in the dharma of a householder? Having spoken these words, Ananta departed. When another thousand years had passed, he returned once more and addressed him in the same manner. When this was said, the Brahmin replied to the sage, "Truly, O Blessed One, I do take delight in the dharma of a householder. Upon hearing this, the great seer went away again. Later, approaching once more, he addressed him with those very same words.

The Brāhmaṇa replied to him, "It is even so. But the Great Sage asked, "Are you able to lead the pure life of celibacy, or not? The Brāhmaṇa said, "I am able to live in such a manner. Thereupon, abandoning the duties of a householder, he practiced the conduct of a wandering ascetic and became a disciple of Kapila.

The opponent asks: For what reason has this inquiry arisen in this Brahmin? He provides the answer: From the assault of the threefold suffering. What, then, is the threefold suffering? It is internal (*ādhyātmika*), external (*ādhibhautika*), and celestial (*ādhidaivika*). Among these, the internal is that suffering of disease which arises from the imbalance of wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*śleṣman*). As it is stated in the *Cikitsā-tantra*: "Below the navel, the seat of wind is said to be located."

Below the heart is said to be the seat of *pitta*; above the heart, everything is related to *śleṣman* (phlegm). When *vāta* becomes aggravated, it overcomes *śleṣman* and *pitta* and produces a disease of wind (*vātaroga*). *Pitta* and *śleṣman* likewise [overcome *vāta*]. This is called bodily suffering (*śārīra-duḥkha*). Mental suffering (*mānasa-duḥkha*) consists of separation from the beloved, union with the unpleasant, and failure to obtain what is desired; these three types constitute mental suffering. Such suffering is designated as internal suffering (*ādhyātmika-duḥkha*).

The *ādhibhautika* (pertaining to other beings) is that suffering which arises from the destruction of mortals, animals, birds, serpents, embankments, and so forth; this is called *ādhibhautika* suffering. The *ādhidaivika* (pertaining to divine or supernatural causes) is that which is of various kinds—cold, heat, wind, rain, lightning, and the like—and which pierces the vital points (*marman*); this is designated as *ādhidaivika* suffering. From the affliction caused by these three types of suffering, there arises the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) regarding the cause that strikes down suffering.

The opponent says: This twofold cause for the destruction of the threefold suffering is clearly perceptible. The first, as taught in the *Aṣṭāṅgāyurveda*, is the destroyer of bodily suffering. The second consists of the six pleasant objects of sense, which are the destroyers of mental suffering. These two causes are indeed directly perceived. How, then, can there be a desire to know (*jijñāsā*)? It is replied: this position is not tenable because of the existence of two kinds of defects. The desire to know is not contrary to reason.
And those two kinds of defects are the non-conclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) and the non-finality (*anātyantikatā*) of the cause. (1)

The opponent says: If the eight-limbed Ayurveda and so forth, being associated with two defects, are not sufficient as a cause for the destruction of suffering, there exists, however, another cause in the four Vedas. This cause brings about a result that is both certain and absolute. Therefore, your desire to investigate [Ayurveda] is useless. For it is said in the Veda:
"We have drunk the Soma, we have become immortal, we have reached the light, we have found the gods.
What can hostility now do to us? And what can the malice of a mortal do to the immortal? Thus it is said.

He states the answer: "The scriptural (ānuśravika) [means] is like the perceptible (dṛṣṭa), for it is characterized by impurity, decay, and excess; superior to that is the [means] which is the opposite, arising from the discernment of the Manifest, the Unmanifest, and the Knower. (2)

The visible cause (*dṛṣṭa-hetu*) as described in Āyurveda is characterized by the defects of being non-conclusive (*anaikāntika*) and non-absolute (*anātyantika*). The revealed cause (*ānuśravika-hetu*) is that which is obtained through hearing the instruction, beginning from Brahmā down to the great sage Kapila; therefore, the four Vedas are called "revealed. These Vedas are also defective in two ways, just as the visible [cause] in Āyurveda is. Furthermore, they possess three defects: impurity (*aviśuddhi*), as it is said in the Veda:
"O beast, may your father, mother, and all your kinsmen give you their permission!"
"Having abandoned this body, you shall obtain birth in heaven.
As it is said in the *Aśvamedha*:
"Six hundred animals are slaughtered; six hundred minus three animals [are required]."

If they are even less than that, then they do not attain birth in heaven for the sake of the fivefold experiences such as bliss. If a man should speak untruth, the gods and great sages say, "This is no sin. Such sins exist within the cause that is revealed by sacred tradition (*ānuśravika*). Therefore, it is impure and subject to decay, as it is said in the Veda:
"All things pass away with time; for time is indeed difficult to overcome."

When this merit (*dharma*) is exhausted, the donor returns from heaven; therefore, it is characterized by decay (*kṣaya*). It is characterized by relative superiority (*atiśaya*): for example, a poor man suffers upon seeing a wealthy man; an ugly person suffers upon seeing one who is handsome, and a fool suffers upon seeing a wise man. Likewise, even in heaven, those of inferior rank suffer upon seeing those of superior rank. Therefore, it is characterized by superiority. These three—along with the two previously mentioned [decay and effort]—make five defects; thus, the Veda is not the cause for the destruction of suffering.

The opponent asks: "What is the superior cause? He provides the answer: "That which is contrary to these two types of causes is superior. These two causes are those mentioned in Āyurveda and those mentioned in the Vedas—namely, that which is absolute (*aikāntika*), ultimate (*ātyantika*), pure (*viśuddha*), inexhaustible (*akṣaya*), and equal (*samāna*). Therefore, it is superior to the former two. The opponent asks: "From where is this cause obtained? He provides the answer: "From the discriminative knowledge of the Manifest (*vyakta*), the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), and the Knower (*jña*)."

The Manifest consists of the Great Principle (mahat), ego-consciousness (ahaṅkāra), the five subtle elements (tanmātra), the five organs of action, the five organs of perception, the mind (manas), and the five gross elements. These seven are called the Manifest because they are produced from primordial nature (prakṛti). The Unmanifest is Pradhāna, the root cause. The Knower is the Puruṣa. For those who possess knowledge of these twenty-five principles as objects of cognition, there is neither increase nor decrease; rather, there occurs absolute liberation from the threefold suffering. As it is said in a verse concerning liberation:
"One who knows the twenty-five principles may dwell in whatever stage of life (āśrama) he may."

"Whether one has matted hair, a shaven head, or a topknot, one is liberated; there is no doubt in this. Thus the opponent said. [The author] asks: "How is the distinction between the root-nature (mūlaprakṛti), the transformations (vikṛti), and the spirit (puruṣa)? He provides the answer: "The root-nature is not a transformation; the seven beginning with the Great One (mahat) are both natures and transformations."
The group of sixteen, however, is a modification; the Puruṣa is neither nature nor a modification. || 3 ||

The primal nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) is the mother of all. It is designated as "primal nature" because it is not produced from anything else. The primal nature receives the name "root" (*mūla*) because it is the generator of the Great One (*mahat*) and the others. It is an unevolved principle (*avikṛti*) because it is not produced from anything else. The Great One, the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*): these seven are both evolvents (*prakṛti*) and evolutions (*vikṛti*). The Great One is an evolution because it is produced from the primal nature; it is an evolvent because it generates the five subtle elements.

The five subtle elements (*tanmātras*) are *vikṛtis* (evolutes) because they are produced from the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*). They are *prakṛtis* (evolvents) because they produce the gross elements (*mahābhūtas*) and the sense organs (*indriyas*). Among these, the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*) is a *prakṛti* because it generates space (*ākāśa*) and the auditory organ; likewise, up to the subtle element of smell (*gandhatanmātra*), which generates earth (*pṛthivī*) and the olfactory organ. Thus, all seven are both *prakṛtis* and *vikṛtis*. The group of sixteen, however, consists exclusively of *vikāras* (modifications).

The five great elements beginning with space, the five sense organs beginning with hearing, the five organs of action beginning with speech, and the mind—these sixteen factors are indeed only modifications (*vikāra*), because they are produced from something else and do not produce anything else. The *puruṣa* is neither primordial nature (*prakṛti*) nor a modification. Here, *puruṣa* refers to the Self (*ātman*), because its essence is consciousness. That Self is neither a producer nor produced from anything else; being distinct from the preceding triad [of nature, intellect, and ego], it is neither nature nor a modification. (3)

An opponent asks: By what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are these three categories—the manifest (*vyakta*), the unmanifest (*avyakta*), and the knower (*jña*)—made known? For in the world, a means of valid cognition is that which is capable of making known the object of cognition (*prameya*). Just as scales, measuring rods, and so forth make known length, shortness, heaviness, or lightness. The reply states: Perception (*dṛṣṭa*), inference (*anumāna*), and authoritative verbal testimony (*āptavacana*)—these three are accepted as the means of valid cognition because all means of valid cognition are established within them. Indeed, the establishment of the objects of cognition depends upon the means of valid cognition. (Sāṅkhyakārikā 4)

In this treatise, threefold means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are established: perception (*dṛṣṭa*), inference (*anumāna*), and authoritative testimony (*āptavacana*). Perception is the means of valid cognition produced from the contact of the sense organs with their objects; that which is revealed by such knowledge, being non-erroneous and free from doubt, is called perception. Inference is the means of valid cognition preceded by perception. It is of three kinds: *pūrvavat* (based on what precedes), *śeṣavat* (based on what remains), and *sāmānyato dṛṣṭa* (based on general observation).

This object which is not apprehended through the two means of valid cognition, perception and inference, is nevertheless apprehended through the word of a reliable person (*āptavacana*). For example, heaven and the northern direction (*uttarāvatī*): this object is not apprehended by perception or inference, yet it is apprehended through the word of a reliable person. Regarding the word of a reliable person, as stated in the verse: "Tradition (*āgama*) is indeed the word of a reliable person; one is considered reliable due to the destruction of faults.
One whose faults are destroyed would not speak an untrue statement, because the cause for doing so is absent."

They make known all objects of knowledge (*prameya*). Whatever remains as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and whatever remains as an object of knowledge (*prameya*), all of this is not outside these three types of means of valid cognition. This is because the six means of valid cognition, such as comparison (*upamāna*) and so forth, are included within authoritative testimony (*āptavacana*). "The establishment of objects of knowledge is from the means of valid cognition" means that since all things are subsumed within the twenty-five categories (*padārtha*) which are the objects of knowledge, their "establishment" (*siddhi*) is the cognition of these twenty-five categories. How do they receive the name "object of knowledge"?

Because it is the object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is established as the "object of cognition" (*prameya*). By means of perception, inference, and authoritative verbal testimony, the three categories [of manifest, unmanifest, and the knower] are briefly established; however, they are expanded into twenty-five types. (4)

An opponent says: "The three kinds of means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) have been mentioned. What is the definition of a means of valid cognition? He provides the answer: "Perception is the ascertainment of each respective object; inference is declared to be of three kinds, preceded by the mark (liṅga) and the bearer of the mark (liṅgin); and authoritative verbal testimony is the word of a reliable person. (5)

"Perception (*dṛṣṭa*) is the ascertainment (*adhyavasāya*) of each respective object. The ear produces an ascertainment regarding sound; likewise, up to the nose, which produces an ascertainment regarding odor. It is precisely an instrument of ascertainment, not a mere indicator; this is called the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) known as perception. "Inference (*anumāna*) is threefold, being 'known' (*jñāta*). Namely: that which has a prior [cause] (*pūrvavat*), that which has a remainder (*śeṣavat*), and that which is perceived through general correlation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*).

This threefold knowledge, having perception as its cause, is capable of distinguishing between the three types of objects of knowledge (*prameya*) and the three times (*adhvan*); this is called inference (*anumāna*). For example, upon seeing a dark cloud, one might know that rain will certainly occur; or, upon seeing fresh, muddy water overflowing in a river, one might know that rain has certainly fallen upstream.

Or, for example, having seen a mango tree in full bloom in Pāṭalipura, one might know that it is likewise so in the country of Kośala. "Preceded by the mark (liṅga) and the bearer of the mark (liṅgin)" means that the mark is conjoined with the bearer of the mark and not separated from it; through the perception of the mark, the inference of the probandum (sādhya) is established. "The scripture of a reliable person" is called the word of a reliable person (āptavacana), such as the four Vedas and the Dharmaśāstra spoken by Brahmā and Manu. || 5 ||

The opponent says: "Three kinds of inference have been stated. Among these, by which means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the establishment of which object of cognition (*prameya*) understood? He provides the answer: "But from that which is seen in a general way, there is the comprehension of supersensible things through inference;
and what is beyond perception and not established even by that is established through authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*). (6)

"Generalized observation" (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*) refers to that which is called "generalized observation" among the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). [The two], primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and the spirit (*puruṣa*), are objects beyond the senses; therefore, this means of valid cognition, generalized observation, establishes them. The effects such as the Great One (*mahat*) and so forth consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion, and are thus endowed with the three qualities (*guṇas*). These are the qualities of the effect. Without the qualities of the primary cause (*pradhāna*), the qualities of the effect cannot be established. Therefore, the primary cause is inferred by means of the qualities of the effect.

Therefore, *prakṛti* (primordial nature) is established through inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭānumāna*). The *puruṣa* (spirit) must likewise be engaged with exclusively; because the transformations such as the *mahat* and so forth exist for the sake of another, the *puruṣa* is also established by inference based on general observation. If any object is not established through either perception or inference, then, because it lies outside the scope of knowledge arising from those two, it is determined by the word of a reliable authority (*āptavacana*), such as "Śakra is the lord of the gods" and so forth. || 6 ||

The opponent says: "Prakṛti and Puruṣa do not exist, because they are not perceived, just as a non-existent person has two heads or three arms. This is resolved: there are eight kinds of non-perception of objects that actually exist. What are the eight kinds? He demonstrates them through a verse: "Due to excessive distance, due to proximity, due to injury of the senses, due to instability of the mind, due to subtlety, due to obstruction, due to being overwhelmed, and due to intermixture with similar things. (7)

In the world, there is non-perception of things that actually exist due to extreme distance, such as the non-perception of objects fallen into the far distance across a riverbank; non-perception due to proximity, such as the failure to grasp an object situated in the eye; non-perception due to impairment of the sense faculties, such as when the deaf and the blind do not perceive sound and form; non-perception due to instability of the mind, such as when one whose mind is directed toward another object does not perceive the object present before them; and non-perception due to subtlety.

Just as the subtle atoms of smoke, heat, mist, and frost situated in the sky are not perceived; [this is] non-perception due to obstruction (*vyavadhāna*), just as an object hidden by a wall is not perceived. Non-perception due to being overwhelmed (*abhibhava*): just as when the sun rises, the stars and the moon do not shine. Non-perception due to the blending with the similar (*samānābhihāra*): just as a bean within a heap of beans, being of the same kind, is difficult to discern.

Thus, there is a non-apprehension of existing things in eight ways. There is also a fourfold non-apprehension of non-existing things: non-apprehension due to prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*); for example, when a vessel has not yet been made from clay, the vessel is not apprehended. Non-apprehension due to non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*); for example, once a jar is destroyed, it is no longer apprehended. Non-apprehension due to mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*); for example, horse-ness is not seen in a cow, nor is cow-ness seen in a horse.

Non-perception results from absolute non-existence; for example, a non-Lord having two heads or three arms. Thus, there are twelve kinds of non-perceptions regarding both existing and non-existing things. Therefore, what you have stated—that primordial matter (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa) do not exist because they are not perceived—is not tenable. || 7 ||

The opponent says: "If primordial matter (prakṛti) and the spirit (puruṣa) are not perceived, which two among the twelve [categories] are not perceived? It is resolved: They are not perceived for one reason. What is that one reason? He demonstrates it through the noble verse: "Because of its subtlety, there is no perception of it; it is not due to non-existence. Its perception occurs through its effects. And those effects, beginning with the Great One (mahat), are both dissimilar and similar to primordial matter. (SK 8)

"Nature (prakṛti) is not perceived because of its subtlety; it is not the case that an unperceived cause is non-existent. Thus, the Pradhāna exists but is not perceived due to its subtlety, just as smoke [or] atoms are not perceived because of their subtlety; so too is the Pradhāna. It is not, however, like a second head or a third arm, which is not perceived because of absolute non-existence. The opponent asks: "If it is not perceived, how then is it known to exist? It is replied:

An effect is observed in dependence upon its own cause. By means of inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭānumāna*)—that an effect is produced by a primary cause—it is known that the Pradhāna exists. The opponent asks: "What is that effect? It is replied: "The Great One (*mahat*) and so forth are its effects. From the Pradhāna, the Great One arises; from the Great One, the I-principle (*ahaṅkāra*); from the I-principle, the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*); and from the five subtle elements, the sixteen transformations arise. The effect, beginning with the Great One, is seen to consist of the three qualities (*triguṇa*)."

Therefore, it is known that the Pradhāna consists of the three guṇas. It is both dissimilar to and similar to its nature (prakṛti). The effect is of two kinds: dissimilar to its nature and similar to its nature. Just as when two sons are born to one man, one is similar to his father and the other is dissimilar to him; so too this effect, which has that [Pradhāna] as its cause, is both similar to and dissimilar from its nature. This will be explained in detail later. Such is the nature of the effect in this treatise. (8)

Here we ask: if disciples are to be instructed, does the effect—such as a jar—exist in the lump of clay and so forth, or does it not exist, or is it both existent and non-existent? Why is this so? Because of the differences in the views of the teachers. Some teachers say that the effect, such as a jar, exists within the lump of clay and so forth. The Vaiśeṣikas say that the effect is non-existent prior to its production and comes into being afterwards. The Śākyas, however, have stated: "In the lump of clay, the jar neither exists nor does it not exist."

Because these three have been stated in three ways, [the argument] is resolved as follows: first, we shall refute the Śākya position; afterwards, we shall refute the Vaiśeṣika position. As for what the Śākyas say—that "it is neither existent nor non-existent"—that is not tenable, because of the contradiction inherent in its own nature. If it is "not existent," then it is established as non-existent. If it is "not non-existent," then it is established as existent. Thus, it cannot be established that it is both existent and non-existent, because of the mutual contradiction within a single locus.
As someone has said: "This person is dead and yet he lives. This statement is mutually contradictory and therefore not sound. The word of the Śākyas is likewise.

(It is stated in the Tripiṭaka: This position is not logical. Why? Because such a doctrine is impossible for the Śākyas. When they say "it is not existent," it is not a doctrine of non-existence; when they say "it is not non-existent," it is not a doctrine of existence. Since they have abandoned both the doctrines of existence and non-existence, their refutation is not established.)

Now we shall refute the Vaiśeṣika doctrine. The Vaiśeṣikas are mistaken; in our view, however, the effect is necessarily contained within the cause, and thus he demonstrates the five reasons [for the pre-existence of the effect]. What are the five reasons? "Because that which is non-existent cannot be produced, because there is a selection of a material cause, because there is no possibility of everything arising from everything, because the capable [cause] produces only what it is capable of producing, and because of the nature of the cause—the effect exists [in the cause]. (Verse 9)

"Because that which is non-existent cannot be produced. For in the world, the production of what is non-existent is not established; for example, oil from sand. The production of what is existent is possible; for example, the emergence of oil through the pressing of sesame seeds. If the effect did not exist here [in the cause], it would not arise. We indeed observe that the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest are born from Primordial Matter (pradhāna); therefore, it is known that the Great Principle and the rest exist within Primordial Matter. "And because one necessarily takes up a material cause. If someone desires an effect, [they must take up its cause].

One necessarily takes up a material cause for that purpose, just as someone thinks: "Tomorrow Brahmins will eat at my house; therefore, I shall take milk today. If there were no curd in the milk, why would he not take water instead? From the fact that one who seeks an effect takes up a specific material cause, it is known that the Great Principle (*mahat*) exists within the Primal Matter (*pradhāna*). This is because of the possibility of everything arising [from it]. If the effect did not exist in the cause, then anything could produce everything.

[If it were otherwise,] grass, stones, sand, and so forth would produce gold, silver, and the like. From the impossibility of such an effect [arising from such causes], it is known that the effect exists within the cause; for "the capable produces only what is possible. Just as a potter, equipped with the necessary implements, fashions jars, bowls, and the like from a lump of clay—things that are possible [to produce from it]—but does not produce a jar or a bowl from grass, trees, or the like; so too, the Pradhāna, being capable, produces the Mahat and the other principles. Therefore, it is known that the Mahat and the rest exist within the Pradhāna.

Because the effect exists in accordance with its cause; that is, whatever the nature of the cause, the effect is of that same nature. For example, a barley sprout necessarily follows the genus of barley. If the effect were non-existent [prior to production], then the effect would necessarily be dissimilar to its cause. This being the case, a sprout of mung beans and the like could arise from barley. Since such a thing is impossible, it is known that the effect pre-exists [in the cause]. The Vaiśeṣikas and others say that the effect does not exist in the cause; this is not tenable. Therefore, it is known that the effect is invariably present in the cause. || 9 ||

Having concluded the intermediate questions, the previously mentioned subject is introduced once more with the words "the Manifest is dissimilar to Nature. Dissimilarity is ninefold: "The Manifest is caused, non-eternal, non-pervasive, active, manifold, dependent, indicative, composite, and subordinate; the Unmanifest is the opposite. (Kārikā 10)

"Having a cause" means that everything from the Great One (mahat) down to the five gross elements has a cause. For instance: Pradhāna is the cause of the Great One; the Great One is the cause of the ego (ahaṅkāra); the ego is the cause of the five subtle elements (tanmātra); and the five subtle elements are the causes of the sixteen principles beginning with the sense organs. Pradhāna, however, is not like this, because it is not produced from a cause. Therefore, it is said to be "dissimilar. "Impermanent" means that the Great One and the rest are produced from Pradhāna; because they are produced, they are impermanent.

Impermanence is of two kinds: impermanence as lasting for a short time (*acirakālāvasthāyin*) and momentary impermanence (*kṣaṇikānitya*). That which exists for as long as a contrary cause has not yet arrived is "lasting for a short time," such as mountains, forests, and so forth. When the danger of fire has not yet arrived, it remains for a brief period; but when the danger of fire arrives, the five great elements (*pañcamahābhūta*) dissolve into the five subtle elements (*pañcatanmātra*). The five subtle elements dissolve into the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*); the ego-principle dissolves into the Great Principle (*mahat*).

The Great One (*mahat*) dissolves into the Primal Matter (*pradhāna*). Therefore, this [Great One] and the subsequent principles are impermanent; the Primal Matter is not so, because it is eternal and because it does not dissolve [into anything else]. "Multiple": the Great One and the rest are multiple, because they differ with respect to each individual *puruṣa*. The ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) is likewise. The Primal Matter, however, is only one, because it is common to many *puruṣas*. "Non-pervasive": the Primal Matter and the *puruṣas* pervade everywhere—on earth, in the intermediate space, and in heaven—but the effects such as the Great One do not do so, because they are not omnipresent.

Therefore, it is distinct from primordial nature (*prakṛti*). It is active: desiring to bring forth the world-process (*saṃsāra*) consisting of effects such as the Great Principle (*mahat*) and so forth, it causes the subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīra*)—by means of the thirteenfold instruments—to wander in the world-process; it expands and contracts it, and it causes it to go and come. Primordial nature (*pradhāna*) is not like this, because contraction and expansion are impossible for it. It is called "the mark" (*liṅga*): when the modifications beginning with the Great Principle have ceased with respect to primordial nature, it is no longer perceived; this is what is designated as the "mark."

Just as the five great elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth attain dissolution (*laya*) into the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), we no longer perceive the great elements and so forth; likewise, the Great One (*mahat*) dissolves into primordial matter (*pradhāna*), and even the Great One is no longer perceived. Primordial matter, however, is not like that, because it lacks the state of attaining dissolution. It is "possessed of parts" (*sāvayava*): everything beginning with the Great One is possessed of parts because its constituent parts are distinct. Primordial matter is not like that, because it is eternal and because it lacks constituent parts. It is "dependent" (*āśrita*).

The Great One (*mahat*) rests upon the Primal Nature (*pradhāna*); the Ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) rests upon the Great One; the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*) rest upon the Ego-sense; and the entire group of sixteen, beginning with the five gross elements, rests upon the five subtle elements. The Primal Nature does not [rest] in such a manner, because it is not produced by anything else. It is "dependent" (*paratantra*) because the effects produced from the Primal Nature, such as the Great One and the rest, lack independence—just as a son is not independent while his father is alive. The Primal Nature is not like that.
Because the cause lacks dependence on anything else; by these nine kinds of causes, it is said that there is a dissimilarity between the manifest and the unmanifest due to their difference. || 10 ||
Having stated the dissimilarity (*vairūpya*), the similarity (*sārūpya*) is now being declared. He demonstrates this through the verse beginning with "prakṛtisārūpyam":

"The Manifested (*vyakta*) is composed of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), non-discriminative (*aviveki*), objective (*viṣaya*), common (*sāmānya*), insentient (*acetana*), and productive (*prasavadharmin*); so too is Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*). The Spirit (*puruṣa*) is the opposite of these, and likewise [is the Unmanifest]. (11)
Thus, the Pradhāna and the Vyakta are similar, whereas the Puruṣa is the opposite of both similarity and dissimilarity.

Homogeneity is sixfold. Among these, the first is "the Manifested possesses the three qualities. The Manifested possesses the three qualities. By "Manifested" is meant the Great Principle (*mahat*), the I-principle (*ahaṅkāra*), and so on, up to the five gross elements (*mahābhūta*). This thirteenfold category is entirely composed of the three qualities: *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Because the Manifested possesses the three qualities, it is known that the Unmanifested also possesses the three qualities; for the effect is not distinct from its cause, just as a black cloth [is produced] from black threads.

Because the cause and the effect possess the same nature (*sārūpya*), the Manifest (*vyakta*) is known to consist of the three *guṇas*. And because the Manifest is produced by the Unmanifest (*pradhāna*), the Unmanifest is also known to consist of the three *guṇas*; thus, the similarity between the Manifest and the Unmanifest has been stated. Regarding "non-discriminative" (*aviveki*): it is not possible to distinguish the Manifest from the *guṇas*, just as a cow and a horse are distinct entities. However, the *guṇas* and the Manifest are not so distinct; likewise, the Unmanifest, though consisting of the three *guṇas*, is similarly non-discriminative. Thus, the Manifest and the Unmanifest are similar. Regarding "object" (*viṣaya*): [it is that which is experienced].

The manifest, beginning with the Great One (mahat), is called an "object" because it is to be experienced by the Puruṣa; the Pradhāna is also like that, because it is to be experienced by the Puruṣa. Regarding "commonality": the manifest, beginning with the Great One, is useful in common to all Puruṣas, just as one female slave may have many masters, since she is to be employed in common by all of them. Likewise, the Pradhāna is also useful in common to all Puruṣas; therefore, it is said to be "of the same form. Regarding "insentient": [Note: The provided text contains a mix of Sanskrit and English. The translation above renders the Sanskrit portions into English while preserving the technical terminology.]

The Manifest, beginning with the Great One (mahat), does not discern the distinctions of pleasure, pain, and delusion, because cognition is acquired solely by the Puruṣa. Properties distinct from the Puruṣa are insentient; the Pradhāna is likewise so. Both the Manifest and the Unmanifest are equal in being insentient; their state is of the same nature. Thus, the Pradhāna and the Manifest are similar in having the property of productivity: the Mahat produces the Ahaṅkāra; the Ahaṅkāra produces the five subtle elements (tanmātras), up to the five gross elements.

"Pradhāna produces Mahat"—this is the similarity between the manifest (vyakta) and the unmanifest (avyakta). "The Puruṣa is the opposite of both similarity and dissimilarity. There is a sixfold similarity between the manifest and the unmanifest; the Puruṣa does not possess this similarity. Therefore, he is "opposite to similarity" and "opposite to dissimilarity. A ninefold dissimilarity has been stated for the manifest and the unmanifest; therein, the Puruṣa is the opposite of eight kinds. Thus it is said that he is "opposite to dissimilarity.
Because there is a plurality of Puruṣas, there is no similarity with Pradhāna. (11)

The opponent says: It has been stated that the manifest and the unmanifest consist of the three *guṇas*. Of what nature are these three *guṇas*? He answers with the following verse: "The *guṇas* consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion; their purposes are illumination, activity, and restraint; and they function by mutually suppressing, supporting, producing, and consorting with one another. (12)

"Consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion": these three qualities are *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Pleasure is the nature of *sattva*; pain is the nature of *rajas*; delusion is the nature of *tamas*. Thus, three inherent dispositions are observed. "For the purposes of illumination, activity, and restraint": what do these three qualities perform? The first (*sattva*) is capable of producing illumination and light; the middle one (*rajas*), however, is capable of producing activity and impulse.

The last [of the three] is capable of performing the restriction and bondage. This is the effect characterized by the three *guṇas*. Furthermore, the properties of the three *guṇas* consist of mutual suppression, support, production, and companionship. What are the properties of the three *guṇas*? Their properties are fivefold. Regarding "mutual suppression": if *sattva* is predominant, it suppresses *rajas* and *tamas*, just as the great sunbeam suppresses the moon, the stars, and so forth.

If *rajas* is predominant, it overcomes *sattva* and *tamas*; just as the shining rays of the sun overpower the stars and the moon. If *tamas* is predominant, it overcomes *rajas* and *sattva*; just as by the great light of the sun, the light of the stars and the moon is no longer seen. Regarding "mutual dependence": these qualities (*guṇas*) depend upon one another and are capable of performing all functions.

Just as a triple-staff (tridaṇḍī) supports a water-pot and other objects by relying on one another; and regarding "mutual production": sometimes *sattva* produces *rajas* and *tamas*; sometimes *rajas* produces *sattva* and *tamas*; and sometimes *tamas* produces *rajas* and *sattva*. Just as three men, supporting one another, simultaneously perform a single task, so too the qualities (*guṇas*) residing in the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest, supporting one another, perform birth and death through their combination.

Regarding the phrase "mutually paired": *sattva* is sometimes paired with *rajas*, and sometimes with *tamas*; *rajas* is sometimes paired with *sattva*, and sometimes with *tamas*; likewise, *tamas* is also sometimes paired with *sattva*, and sometimes with *rajas*. As stated in the verse by the great seer Vyāsa:
"Sattva is the mate of rajas, and rajas is the mate of sattva;
both sattva and rajas are said to have tamas as their mate."

Regarding the phrase "mutually functioning": these three qualities (*guṇas*) perform their functions for one another. For example, a woman in a royal household who possesses a most pleasing appearance and character—this is called the quality of *sattva*. This form, as it transforms from *sattva*, produces joy in her husband and kinsmen; this is called performing one's own purpose (*svārthakaraṇa*). [That same woman] generates grief in all her co-wives; this is called performing the purpose of others (*anyārthakaraṇa*). She also generates despondency in others.

Just as female slaves and others, constantly exhausted by their service and unable to obtain liberation, become possessed of minds filled with despondency—this is called "producing the welfare of another. This very act is said to be the performance of the welfare of both self and others by the quality of *sattva*. *Rajas* produces the welfare of both self and others; for example, when a certain thief binds a woman of the royal household, a member of the royal lineage arrives mounted on a horse, takes up a staff, and rescues her. That member of the royal lineage is a transformation of *rajas*.

Even one belonging to a royal lineage, though within the sphere of fear, experiences joy thinking, "I shall obtain release from the women"; this is the production of another purpose. Other thieves, upon seeing the king, do not move, remaining like a pillar; this is called the production of delusion in others. It has been stated that *rajas* produces [results] for both self and others. *Tamas* also produces [results] for both self and others; just as a great, dark cloud initiates lightning and so forth, the cloud being a transformation of *tamas*.

All farmers who live by their crops rejoice; this is called "producing another's purpose. It also produces delusion (*moha*); for example, a certain young woman separated from her husband, seeing this cloud and lightning, grieves, thinking, "My husband has not returned. That the cloud produces delusion in women is called "producing one's own purpose. It also produces sorrow (*śoka*).

Just as merchants traveling on a road become drenched, unable to carry their loads, and weary of heart; this is called "producing another purpose. In this way, the fivefold attributes (dharmas) are associated with the three qualities (guṇas). || 12 ||
Furthermore, there is the defining characteristic of the qualities (guṇas):
Sattva is held to be light and illuminating; rajas is stimulating and mobile; tamas is heavy and enveloping. Their functioning is for the sake of a purpose, like a lamp. (13)

"Sattva is held to have the characteristics of lightness and illumination. Light means subtle; illumination means that which makes things manifest. That is what is called *sattva*. If *sattva* is predominant, all the sense organs become light, supple, and capable of grasping their objects; then one should consider that *sattva* is predominant. "Rajas is held to have the characteristics of stimulation and mobility. Stimulation means being restless and disregarding other [qualities].

Just as a rutting elephant, seeking a conflict, encounters and confronts an opposing elephant; so too, when the quality of *rajas* is predominant, a person constantly seeks out quarrels. His mind is perpetually restless and incapable of remaining fixed in one place. In such a case, it should be understood that the *rajas* quality is predominant. As for *tamas*, its characteristic is heaviness and obscuration. When the *tamas* quality is predominant, the entire body is heavy, and the sense organs, being shrouded by *tamas*, are incapable of perceiving their objects.

Then it should be understood that the quality of *tamas* (darkness) prevails in its intensity. An opponent objects: "Even though the qualities (*guṇas*) are mutually contradictory, they nevertheless attain a single simultaneous function because they are not independent, being dependent upon a single person. It is like the conjunction of things that are mutually contradictory for the purpose of a lamp. For three substances, though mutually contradictory, come together for the sake of a lamp: fire is contradictory to both oil and the wick; oil, too, is contradictory to both fire and the wick."
Even so, mutually contradictory objects perform their functions for the sake of human purpose; likewise, the three *guṇas* also perform their functions despite having contradictory natures. (13)

The opponent says: Six points of similarity were previously stated; among them, only one has been perceived by me, while the remaining five have not been perceived. The presence of the three *guṇas* has been established, but the remaining five must also be established. To this, the answer is given in the following verse: Non-discrimination and the rest are established from the fact of the three *guṇas*, because their opposites do not exist.
Since the effect consists of the qualities of its cause, the Unmanifest (*avyakta*) is also established. (14)

"Non-discrimination and so forth are established. The five properties beginning with non-discrimination, as previously stated, are established in the manifest (vyakta) and are likewise established in the primary cause (pradhāna). This is because the effect is established [as being of the same nature]. "Due to the absence of any deviation from the qualities (guṇa) and so forth": since these five properties beginning with non-discrimination are established in the manifest, it is known that they necessarily exist in the primary cause. How is this so? Because of the three qualities (traiguṇya). If the three qualities do not exist separately, then it is known that they are mutually non-discriminative.

If it is non-discriminative, then it should be known as an object (*viṣaya*). If it is called an object, then it should be known as the universal (*sāmānya*). If the universal is accepted, then it is known to be insentient (*acetana*). If it is an object, if it is the universal, and if it is insentient, then it is known to have the property of productivity (*prasavadharmin*). If it is known that these six properties exist in the manifest (*vyakta*), then it is known that those same six properties also exist in the primary cause (*pradhāna*). How is this known?

Because it would be non-existent in the opposite case. If the primordial nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) were excluded, then the effect would not possess its six attributes. Just as if it were set aside from the threads, there would be no cloth distinct from them; wherever there is the substance of the cloth, there alone are the threads. For the thread and the cloth are inseparable. The effect is dependent upon the cause, and the effect and the cause are not distinct. The quality of the effect follows the quality of the cause; therefore, the Unmanifest (*avyakta*) is established.

In this world, all qualities of the effect invariably follow the qualities of the cause, just as a cloth made from black threads invariably follows the blackness of those threads. Likewise, since the manifest and so forth possess the three *guṇas*, it is established that they have five properties. Because the effect possesses six properties, it is known that the unmanifest also possesses these six properties. (14)

The opponent says: "In the world, if an object is not perceived, then that object is considered non-existent, like a second head. Likewise, primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is also not perceived; how then is it known to exist? It is replied: "The weight and the measure of the Himalayas are not known, yet it cannot be said that their measure does not exist. So it is with primordial nature. By what reason can it be known to exist?
Because of the finite measure of the evolved effects (*bheda*), because of their homogeneity (*samanvaya*), and because of the activity of power (*śakti*)."
Because of the distinction between cause and effect, and because of the non-distinction of the manifold universe. || 15 ||

Pradhāna exists. How is this known? Because things of diverse natures possess finite dimensions. In this world, whatever object has an agent, that object is delimited by finite dimensions. For example, a potter produces a jar of delimited dimensions from a lump of clay of finite dimensions. If this jar were without a cause, then the jar would not have delimited dimensions, and the jar would not have been produced at all.

However, a jar is seen to have a limited dimension; therefore, it is known to have a cause, just as cloth and other such things are produced from threads. So too is every object. Among these phenomena (or principles), even the manifest—beginning with the Great One (mahat)—has a limited dimension. What is that limited dimension? It is: the Great One is one, ego (ahaṅkāra) is one, the five subtle elements (tanmātras) are [five], the eleven organs are [eleven], and the five gross elements are [five].

Thus, this Manifest has been seen by us to possess definite dimensions. By means of this inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*), it is known that the Unmanifest (*pradhāna*) must necessarily exist. If the Unmanifest were non-existent, this Manifest would be of unlimited dimensions. Furthermore, what else could be non-existent? Because they share the same essential nature (*svabhāva*). Just as in the case of a piece of sandalwood: even though there are many pieces, the nature of sandalwood is ultimately one and the same in all of them; so too is it with the Manifest.

Among the various evolutes beginning with the Great Principle (mahat), there is a single nature consisting of the three qualities (traiguṇya). Because they possess this single nature, it is known that all of them have a cause; therefore, it is known that Pradhāna exists. And because activity proceeds from power: whatever is capable of something engages in that [activity]. Just as a potter, being capable of making pots and small jars, engages in the production of pots and small jars, but does not engage in the production of cloth and so forth. This small jar, while being produced, is established by depending upon a specific power.

And that power (śakti) necessarily has a substratum, namely, the potter. The same applies to the manifest (vyakta). The manifest possesses activity (pravṛtti); this activity is accomplished by means of power. And that power has a substratum; the substratum of that [power] is Pradhāna. From the fact that activity proceeds from power, it is known that Pradhāna exists. This is because of the distinction between cause and effect. In the world, the distinction between cause and effect is observed: for example, a lump of clay is the cause, and the jar and so forth are the effects.

This jar is capable of holding water, oil, and so forth, but a lump of clay is not. This is the distinction between cause and effect. The same applies to threads and cloth. Likewise, the manifest (vyakta), such as the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest, must necessarily be an effect. Observing this effect, we know that there exists a distinct, dissimilar cause. Therefore, Pradhāna exists. Regarding the phrase "due to the non-differentiation of the multiformity" (vaiśvarūpyasyāvibhāgāt): furthermore, it is to make known that there is another cause—that Pradhāna exists as a reality—that [the text] says "of the multiformity."

The world is indeed threefold, namely: earth, the intermediate space, and heaven. At the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), the entire world becomes undifferentiated. The five great elements (*mahābhūtas*) and the eleven sense organs dissolve into the five subtle essences (*tanmātras*) and become undifferentiated. When the Great One (*mahat*) dissolves into primordial matter (*pradhāna*), it too becomes undifferentiated; one cannot say, distinguishing them, "this is the manifest" (*vyakta*) and "this is primordial matter. Because the manifest does not exist at the time of dissolution, even primordial matter would become non-existent. If primordial matter does not exist...

Furthermore, cyclic existence (saṃsāra) would not exist; this is not tenable. Since there exists primordial matter (pradhāna), which has the capacity to create the threefold world again, we therefore know that primordial matter exists. Thus, primordial matter is established by means of five reasons. || 15 ||

The opponent says: Even if Pradhāna exists, it is not capable of producing the Manifested (vyakta) because it lacks assistance, just as a single man cannot produce a son, or a single thread cannot produce a cloth; so too with Pradhāna. To this, the Āryā provides the answer: "The Unmanifested cause exists; it proceeds from the three Guṇas and from their combination.
It acts through transformation, like water, due to the specific distinctions based on each respective substratum of the Guṇas. (Verse 16)

"The unmanifest is the cause of the generation of the manifest. This means that because the *pradhāna* is endowed with the three *guṇas*, it is capable of generating the manifest. If these *guṇas* do not belong to the *pradhāna*, then what you have stated would be true. However, if the three *guṇas* do exist, then it is not tenable to say that it cannot generate the manifest due to a lack of conjunction; rather, the three *guṇas* acting in combination generate the manifest.

Just as many threads, when combined, produce a cloth, so too the three *guṇas*, by virtue of being mutually dependent, produce the manifest (*vyakta*). An opponent asks: "In the world, production is of two kinds: that which arises from transformation (*pariṇāmaja*), such as curds produced from milk; and that which does not arise from transformation (*apariṇāmaja*), such as a son born of mother and father. To which of these types of causal production is the manifest, produced from *pradhāna*, assigned? He replies: "By way of transformation, like milk and curds."

The Pradhāna transforms into the Vyakta; that which is the Vyakta is itself the Pradhāna. Therefore, it is not admitted here that [the effect] is produced from something of a different genus. The opponent says: "If there is a single cause, it would not be able to produce a manifold variety of effects. Regarding these matters, if the Pradhāna is one, how could it produce the threefold world? Those born in heaven are happy; those born among humans are suffering; and those born as animals are deluded."

If it arises from a single cause, how is a threefold division obtained? It is explained: like water, due to the specific distinctions of each respective quality (*guṇa*). Celestial water, which initially has but a single taste, reaches the earth; it transforms into various tastes according to the specific differences of its individual vessels.

If it remains in a golden vessel, its taste is exceedingly sweet; if it reaches the earth, the taste becomes manifold and not uniform, following the scent of the earth. In the same way, the threefold world is also not uniform. Although it has arisen from a single primordial matter (*pradhāna*), there is a disparity due to the inequality of the three qualities (*guṇas*). In heaven, the quality of goodness (*sattva*) predominates; therefore, the gods always experience happiness. Among humans, the quality of passion (*rajas*) predominates; therefore, human beings experience much suffering.

In the animal realm, darkness (tamas) is predominant; therefore, animals and the like are always deluded. In all these states of existence, the qualities (guṇas) are always present in conjunction; the distinction [between them] arises from their intensity or lack thereof. Thus, the single Pradhāna produces the three worlds; however, the gradations [of experience] result from the inequality of the three qualities. 16.

The Pradhāna has been explained. Now we shall explain the Puruṣa. Like the Pradhāna, the Puruṣa is subtle. To demonstrate how we know that the Puruṣa exists, he recites this Āryā verse: "Because composite objects exist for the sake of another; because of the reversal of the three guṇas and so forth; because of [the need for] a presiding presence; because there must be an experiencer; and because of the activity for the sake of liberation—the Puruṣa exists. (17)
Because there must be an experiencer and because of the activity for the sake of liberation—these five reasons establish that the Puruṣa exists.

"Because it is for the sake of another in an aggregate. Just as liberation is obtained through the knowledge of the manifest, the unmanifest, and the Knower (*jña*), so it was stated in the first verse. Furthermore, the five reasons establishing the existence of the Primal Nature (*pradhāna*) and the Manifest have been correctly set forth. Now, the extremely subtle Puruṣa must be established. The Puruṣa exists because aggregates exist for the sake of another. For in the world we observe that every aggregate exists for the sake of another.

Just as objects such as beds and seats, being composite wholes, are not for their own sake but are necessarily postulated to be for the sake of another—there being a distinct enjoyer for whose sake these composite structures like houses exist—so too it is with the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest. The body is said to be a composite of the five elements; this body is not for its own sake, but is determined to be exclusively for the sake of another. That "other" is the Puruṣa. Therefore, we know that the Puruṣa exists. Regarding the phrase "due to the reversal of the three qualities": the sixfold similarity between the Pradhāna and the manifest (vyakta) was previously stated in the verse. [As follows:]
"The manifest and the Pradhāna are composed of the three guṇas, non-discriminative, objective, common, insentient, and productive; the Puruṣa is the opposite of these. Thus [it is said].

From the reverse of these six [reasons], it is said that "the Puruṣa exists. Regarding "because of presiding": if the Puruṣa presides over this body, then the body moves; if there were no Puruṣa to preside over the body, then it would not move. As it is stated in the *Ṣaṣṭitantra*: "Presided over by the Puruṣa, the Pradhāna produces the manifest. Therefore, we know that the Puruṣa exists. Regarding "because of being an enjoyer": [the Puruṣa exists].

Just as in the world, upon seeing food and drink possessing the six flavors, it is known that there must be another who eats; so too, upon seeing the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest, it is known that there must necessarily be another enjoyer for whom this is the object of enjoyment. Therefore, we know that the Puruṣa exists. Furthermore, because of the activity for the sake of isolation (kaivalya): if there were only the body, the means to liberation taught by the noble ones would be entirely useless. For example, long ago, a certain seer approached some Brahmins and spoke thus: "All of you possess the wealth of the Vedas, and all of you are drinkers of the Soma."
"Having all seen the face of your own son, do you now desire the dharma of a monk? Thus [he spoke].

If there were only the body, for what purpose would this statement exist? Therefore, we know that the self exists by its very nature as distinct from the body. If there were no other self and only the body existed, then when the bodies of venerable ones—such as mothers, fathers, and teachers—are discarded after death and are burned or buried, and thus treated with such rites, one would incur sin; there would be no merit or virtue. For this reason, we know that there is another, the self. Furthermore, there is the word of the authoritative sages (*āptavacana*).
The marrow and bones are the ropes and pillars; the blood and flesh are the clay and dust.
This body is impure, impermanent, and suffering, while the Lord Self is free from this connection.

"Abandon dharma or even adharma; that which is to be abandoned is the trivial truth. Even the state of renunciation must be abandoned; one who is pure is the sole ruler. If the Self did not exist, liberation (kaivalya) would not occur. From this authoritative scripture, we know with certainty that the Puruṣa exists. Relying on these five reasons, the existence of the Puruṣa has been established. || 17 ||

The opponent asks: Is one *puruṣa* perceived as a single entity collectively throughout many bodies, or is there a distinct *puruṣa* in each body? If it is asked how such a doubt arises, it is because the teachers speak in mutual contradiction. Someone says: One *puruṣa* pervades all bodies, like a thread threading through jewels; there are many jewels, but the thread is one. And just as Viṣṇu, being one, enjoys himself simultaneously with sixty thousand women at one and the same time.

In the same way, the Puruṣa is also one and pervades all bodies. Thus says another teacher, however: "The Self (Ātman) is distinct in every body. Therefore, a doubt has arisen in me. It is resolved: there are many Puruṣas; there is a separate Puruṣa for each body. How is this known? The Ācārya explains through a verse: "Because of the specific determination of birth, death, and the organs, and because of their non-simultaneous activity, as well as from the diversity of the three guṇas, the multiplicity of Puruṣas is established. (Kārikā 18)

"Because of the specific determination of birth, death, and the instruments [of action]. If the Puruṣa were one, then when one is born, all would be born; everywhere, all women would be pregnant, giving birth, having sons, and having daughters simultaneously at one time. But they do not become so; rather, they are distinct in each individual case. Therefore, we know that there are many Puruṣas.

Furthermore, if the Puruṣa were one, then when one dies, all would die; since this is impossible, it is known that the Puruṣa is not one. Furthermore, because of the specific determination of the instruments (karaṇas): if there were only one Puruṣa, then when one person is deaf, all would be deaf; likewise, at one and the same time, all would be blind, mute, one-eyed, and so forth. Since such a state is impossible, it is known that there are many Puruṣas. Furthermore, because of the differentiation of the three guṇas.

If the Puruṣa were one, then the three guṇas would be indistinguishable. For example, just as one Brāhmaṇa father may beget three sons: one who is intelligent and happy, a second who is irritable and miserable, and a third who is characterized by tamas and is deluded. If there were only one Puruṣa, then all would be equally sattvic when one is sattvic; likewise in the case of the miserable and the deluded. Therefore, what you have stated—that the Puruṣa is one, like a string threading jewels or like Viṣṇu—is not tenable.
Therefore, by these five reasons, we know that there are many persons. || 18 ||

Another says: "I have a doubt in this matter: is this person an agent (*kartṛ*) or a non-agent (*akartṛ*)? If it is asked, 'How does this doubt arise?', it is because of worldly convention (*lokavyavahāra*). For the world says, 'The person goes,' 'The person comes,' and 'The person is an agent. The Sāṅkhyas say, 'The person is a non-agent,' while the Vaiśeṣikas say, 'The person is an agent. Therefore, I have a doubt. It is resolved: "The person is a non-agent. How is this known? He explains it through a verse (*āryā*): The person is not an agent; The mind (*citta*) is the agent. The person is the experiencer; The mind is that which experiences. The person is not an agent; the mind is the agent. The person is the experiencer; the mind is that which experiences. Why is this so? Because the person is devoid of mental activity (*cittavṛtti*). Since the person is devoid of mental activity, he is like empty space (*ākāśa*). Just as empty space is not an agent, so too the person is not an agent. Furthermore, the person is eternal and unchanging. If the person were an agent, he would be subject to change, and being subject to change, he would be impermanent. But since the person is eternal and unchanging, he is therefore a non-agent. Moreover, agency belongs to the mind, for the mind is characterized by transformation (*pariṇāma*). Since the mind undergoes transformation, it is the agent. The person, however, is immutable and thus cannot be an agent. Therefore, it is established that the person is a non-agent. This is the definitive conclusion.
And from this absence of error, the witnesshood of this Puruṣa is established, as well as his isolation, neutrality, state of being a seer, and lack of agency. (19)

"From the reversal of the manifest and the unmanifest. In the two preceding Āryā verses it was stated that the *puruṣa* is distinct from *pradhāna* and exceeds the manifest (*vyakta*). This is because of the reversal of those two characteristics—that is, due to its dissimilarity to both. The three *guṇas* are the agents; because he is devoid of those three *guṇas*, the *puruṣa* is a non-agent. An opponent asks: "What is the purpose of this? It is said: for the sake of establishing his status as a witness (*sākṣitva*). The witnesshood of the *puruṣa* is established because the *puruṣa* is the knower.

In this way, no principles (*tattva*) remain [as objects for the Puruṣa]; thus it is called *kaivalya* (isolation). Regarding *mādhyasthya* (neutrality): because the Puruṣa is distinct from both primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and its transformations (*vikāra*), and because he is pure, neutrality is attributed to the Puruṣa. Furthermore, because he is different from the three qualities (*guṇa*), and because the qualities undergo contraction, expansion, and inequality, neutrality is maintained [of the Puruṣa]. Just as a single wandering mendicant, staying alone in one place, does not follow after others coming and going, but merely observes them.

Likewise, the three *guṇas* are capable of contraction, expansion, birth, and death; however, the solitary *puruṣa* merely observes those activities. Therefore, neutrality (*mādhyasthya*) is attributed to him. Because the *puruṣa* is distinct from the transformations of *prakṛti* and because he possesses consciousness, he is called the "seer" (*draṣṭṛ*). He is called the "seer" due to his function as such, but not as a "doer. Thus, the point that the *guṇas* perform actions is established. It is established that the *puruṣa* exists, and that he is manifold and non-active (*akartṛ*). || 19 ||

The opponent says: If the *puruṣa* is not an agent, who performs the resolve (*adhyavasāya*) such as "I shall practice dharma," or "I shall avoid what is undesirable," or "I shall accomplish my vow"? If the three *guṇas* perform that resolve, they would possess consciousness; this is not accepted, because it was previously established that the *guṇas* are insentient. If, on the other hand, the *puruṣa* performs the resolve, then the *puruṣa* would be proven to be an agent.
[And this is not desired] because the non-agency of the Puruṣa was previously established. Therefore, there is a fault in either case. He states the answer in a verse:
"Therefore, through union with that [Puruṣa], the insentient *liṅga* (the subtle body) appears as if it were sentient;
likewise, although the agency belongs to the *guṇas*, the indifferent [Puruṣa] appears as if he were the agent. (20)

"The three *guṇas* arise from conjunction with the *puruṣa*. These *guṇas* are insentient (*acetana*) and act; the *puruṣa* is sentient (*sacetana*) and does not act. Through the conjunction of these two, the *guṇas* become as if they possess sentience. Just as a pot, when heated by fire, becomes hot, and when joined with water, becomes cold; so too the three *guṇas*, conjoined with the sentient one, act as if they possess sentience, performing determination (*adhyavasāya*). Therefore it is said: 'The insentient are as if they possess sentience.'"

As for what you have said—that "the person (puruṣa) is the agent according to worldly convention"—we accept that point. Because of its agency through the three guṇas, the indifferent [puruṣa] becomes as if it were the agent. Due to its conjunction with that [prakṛti], the non-agent is called the "agent. Just as a certain Brahmin, having entered into the midst of a band of thieves by mistake, is seized along with them when they are caught to be executed; because of his going with the thief, he receives the name "thief. In the same way, the person, being bound to the agent, is called "the agent" in worldly convention. || 20 ||

The opponent asks: "By what cause are *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* joined? The Noble One gives the answer in verse: "For the sake of the Puruṣa’s perception, and likewise for the sake of the Pradhāna’s isolation (*kaivalya*), there is a union of both, like that of the lame and the blind; from that, creation proceeds. (21)

"The Puruṣa desires to see the three guṇas. Thus the Puruṣa thinks: "I shall behold the Pradhāna consisting of the three guṇas. For this reason, the Puruṣa joins with the Pradhāna. "The Pradhāna is for the sake of isolation (kaivalya). [The Pradhāna itself thinks: "This wretched Puruṣa is solitary and possesses the power of knowledge and vision; I shall bring him to isolation. For that purpose, the Pradhāna and the Puruṣa join together.

Just as a king is joined with a man [with the thought], "I shall employ this man," and that man is also joined with the king [with the thought], "The king will provide me a livelihood"—therefore, the union between the king and the man is established by the force of purpose—so too is the state of union between *pradhāna* (primordial matter) and the *puruṣa* (spirit). For the sake of the *puruṣa*'s perception and for the sake of the *pradhāna*'s isolation (*kaivalya*), there is a union like that of the lame and the blind. Herein lies the illustration.

Long ago, it is said, a caravan of merchants set out for Ujjayinī when they were attacked by bandits and scattered in various directions. At that time, there was one who was blind from birth and another who was lame from birth; both had been abandoned by everyone else. The blind man, wandering about on all sides, was seen by the lame man as he sat down. The lame man asked, "Who are you? The blind man replied, "I am blind from birth; I do not know by what means I might wander about. But who are you? The lame man replied:

"I am a cripple from birth, capable only of seeing the path, but unable to walk," said the man blind from birth. "Therefore, sit upon my shoulders; I am able to lead the way. You show me the path. Thus, through their mutual cooperation, the two men reached their destination. Their union was brought about by the necessity of the task. Having arrived at their destination, they separated from one another.

In the same way, the Puruṣa attains liberation at the very moment it perceives Pradhāna; and Pradhāna, too, having brought about the isolation (kaivalya) of the Puruṣa, withdraws separately. "The creation of the world is for the sake of an object": the Puruṣa and Pradhāna unite for the purpose of the Puruṣa’s perception of the other and for the sake of Pradhāna’s isolation. This union creates the world, just as a son is produced from the union of both a woman and a man; likewise, the union of Pradhāna and Puruṣa produces the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest. || 21 ||

The opponent says: It has been stated that "conjunction creates the world. But of what nature is this creation? He provides the answer in a verse: "From primordial matter (prakṛti) comes the Great One (mahat); from that, the ego (ahaṅkāra); from that, the group of sixteen;
and from five among those sixteen, the five gross elements arise. (22)

"It is born from *prakṛti* in a sequential order. Here, *prakṛti* is explained as either *pradhāna*, or *brahman*, or that which possesses a manifold nature. If it is born sequentially, then since *prakṛti* is the root, there is nothing else from which it could be born. From *prakṛti*, the *mahat* (the Great One) is produced first. "The Great One" (*mahān*) is explained as intellect (*buddhi*), consciousness (*saṃvitti*), the pervasive one (*vibhu*), thought (*mati*), or wisdom (*prajñā*). Where there is the Great One, there is thought; therefore, the Great One receives the name "thought" (*mati*).

From that, the Great Ego (mahat-ahaṃkāra) is born. This "Ego" is designated as either the *bhūtādi* (the source of elements), the *vaikṛta* (the modified), or the *taijasa* (the radiant). From that Ego, the group of sixteen arises. This "group of sixteen" consists of the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*), the five organs of cognition (*jñānendriyas*), the five organs of action (*karmendriyas*), and the mind (*manas*). The five subtle elements are sound, touch, form, taste, and smell; these are either composed of the five subtle elements or are the potencies of the subtle elements. The five organs of cognition are the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose.

The five organs of action are speech, hands, feet, the generative organ, and the anus. This group of sixteen arises from the *ahaṅkāra* (ego-sense). Therefore it is said: "From the Great Principle (*mahat*) comes the *ahaṅkāra*; from that, the sixteen. Now, within this group of sixteen there are the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*); from these the five gross elements (*mahābhūtas*) are born. Among them, from the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*), the gross element of space (*ākāśa*) arises; from the subtle element of touch (*sparśa-tanmātra*), the gross element of air (*vāyu*) arises; from the subtle element of form (*rūpa-tanmātra*), the gross element of fire (*tejas*) arises.

From the subtle element of taste, the great element of water arises; from the subtle element of smell, the great element of earth arises. I have stated that liberation is attained by perceiving these three principles: primordial nature, its transformations, and the Puruṣa. || 22 ||

The opponent says: It has been stated that the Great Principle (mahat) arises from primordial nature (prakṛti). What are the characteristics of the Great Principle? He provides the answer in a verse: "Determination is intellect (buddhi); [its forms are] virtue, knowledge, dispassion, and power; this is its form when characterized by sattva, while that characterized by tamas is the opposite of this. (23)

"Great determination (*adhyavasāya*) is said to be the Great One (*mahat*). What, indeed, is determination? It is this: "This is a post," or "This is a person. Such a cognition is called determination; determination itself is called the Great One. This Great One has eight limbs: four are *sāttvika* and four are *tāmasa*. The *sāttvika* limbs are as follows: virtue (*dharma*), knowledge (*jñāna*), dispassion (*virāga*), and sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). What is the characteristic of virtue? It consists of the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*). Among these, the restraints are five.

Absence of hatred, honoring the teacher, internal and external purity, moderation in food and drink, and vigilance. There are also five observances (*niyamas*): non-violence, non-stealing, truthfulness, celibacy, and freedom from deceit. These are the ten-fold means (*sādhanas*). Therefore, it is called *dharma*. What is knowledge (*jñāna*)? Knowledge is twofold: external knowledge and internal knowledge. External knowledge consists of the six limbs of the Veda (*ṣaḍ-vedāṅgas*), while internal knowledge is the knowledge of Brahman.

Grammar, ritual codes, astronomy, phonology, etymology—these six branches of knowledge are called the external. Internal knowledge is the realization of the distinction between the three qualities (*guṇas*) and the *puruṣa*. Through external knowledge, worldly success is attained; through internal knowledge, liberation is attained. What is detachment? Detachment is twofold: external and internal. This is the external.

Having observed the afflictions at the times of acquiring, protecting, and exhausting wealth, and having seen the two-fold faults of attachment to protection and violence, one who has become dispassionate through such observation renounces the home and goes forth. One who is dispassionate in this manner does not attain liberation. That dispassion is attained through external knowledge; it is called internal dispassion. Because he has discerned the distinctions between the qualities of the Puruṣa, he desires to go forth. It is that dispassion which is attained preceded by internal knowledge.

Through detachment from that, one attains liberation; through external detachment, however, one remains in saṃsāra. Through internal detachment, one attains liberation. Regarding sovereignty (*aiśvarya*): sovereignty is eightfold. *Aṇimā* is the state of existing like an absolute void. *Laghimā* is the power of becoming extremely light like the mind. *Mahimā* is extreme omnipresence like space. *Prāpti* is the attainment of whatever is desired. *Īśitva* is mastery over the three worlds.

[Prākāmya] is the capacity for the simultaneous enjoyment of objects according to one's desire. [Vaśitva] is the bond of independence; it is the impelling of the beings of the three worlds to carry out commands in accordance with one's own will. [Yathākāmāvasthāyitva] is the attainment of functional activity according to time, place, and mental state—that is, as desired. These four qualities are characterized by *sattva*. If *sattva* is predominant, it overcomes *rajas* and *tamas*.

At this time, because of the predominance of *sattva*, the Puruṣa attains the four qualities beginning with *dharma*; this is the form of *sāttvika*. That which is the reverse of this is *tāmasa*. The opposites of the four forms beginning with *dharma* are: *adharma*, ignorance (*ajñāna*), attachment (*saṃrāgitva*), and lack of sovereignty (*anaiśvarya*). These four qualities are the characteristics of *tāmasa*. Thus, if these four *sāttvika* and four *tāmasa* limbs are conjoined with the Mahat, then the Mahat becomes eight-limbed (*aṣṭāṅga*). This is its primordial state at the time of transformation. || 23 ||
Thus ends the first section of the *Suvarṇasaptatiśāstra*.
Now, in the *Suvarṇasaptati-śāstra*, the Middle Section:
An opponent asks, "The Great One has been mentioned; what is the definition of egoism (*ahaṅkāra*)? The Noble One replies with a verse:
"Egoism is self-conceit (*abhimāna*); from it, the two-fold creation proceeds."
The eleven consisting of the sense organs, and the five subtle elements (tanmātras). || 24 ||

"Ahaṅkāra is self-conceit (abhimāna). What is the definition of ahaṅkāra? That self-conceit which consists of the notions "this sound is mine," "this touch is mine," "this form is mine," "this taste is mine," "this smell is mine," and "this virtuous quality is dear to me"—this is called ahaṅkāra. From that, a twofold creation proceeds. From that ahaṅkāra, a twofold transformation proceeds. What is the twofold [transformation]? The group of eleven consisting of the sense organs, and the five subtle elements (tanmātras) and the five gross elements (mahābhūtas).
The names of the eleven sense organs and the five subtle elements have been stated previously. (24)
The characteristic of ego (ahaṅkāra) has been stated. Ego is threefold. What specific quality arises for each? The answer is given in the Āryā verse:
"From the modified (vaikṛta) ego, the group of eleven [senses] proceeds as sattvic;
from the elemental (bhūtādi) ego, the subtle elements (tanmātra) proceed as tāmasa; and from the fiery (taijasa) ego, both [proceed]. (25)

The elevenfold [set] proceeds from the *sāttvika* *vaikṛta* ego (*ahaṅkāra*). If *sattva* is predominant in the intellect (*buddhi*), then it produces the ego; it overcomes *rajas* and *tamas*. That ego is *sāttvika*; the noble ones call it *vaikṛta*. This *vaikṛta* ego produces the eleven organs. How is this known? Because they abound in *sattva*, are light, luminous, pure, and capable of grasping their respective objects.

Therefore, those eleven are called *sāttvika*. From *bhūtādi*, which is *tāmasa*, the *tanmātras* proceed. If *tamas* is predominant in the *mahat*, then it produces *ahaṅkāra* and overcomes *sattva* and *rajas*. This *ahaṅkāra* is *tāmasa*; therefore, the noble ones call it by the name *bhūtādi*. This *ahaṅkāra* produces the five *tanmātras*. Consequently, all five *tanmātras* and the five great elements (*mahābhūtas*) belong to the *tāmasa* class.

"From the *taijasa* [ego], both proceed. Thus, if *rajas* is predominant in the Great Principle (*mahat*), it then produces the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), while suppressing *sattva* and *tamas*. That ego is of the nature of *rajas* (*rājasa*). Therefore, the noble ones establish its name as *taijasa*. This ego produces both: it produces the eleven organs and the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*s), etc. The *sāttvika-vaikṛtika* ego, which is the producer of the organs, takes the *taijasa* ego as its auxiliary.

How is this so? The *taijasa* (fiery) ego is modified by its active nature; the *sāttvika* (pure) ego is modified by its inactive nature. Therefore, when the ego produces the eleven organs, it necessarily takes the *taijasa* ego as its auxiliary. When the *bhūtādi* (elemental) ego produces the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*) and the five gross elements (*mahābhūtas*), it necessarily takes the *taijasa* ego as its auxiliary. How is this so?
