Because the *tāmasa* ego is inactive and the *taijasa* ego is active, the *taijasa* ego produces the eleven organs and also produces the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*). Therefore it is said: "From the *taijasa*, both proceed. (25)
The opponent says: It has been stated that the *sāttvika* [aspect of *ahaṃkāra*] produces the eleven organs. What are these eleven organs? He provides the answer in a verse:
"The sense organs of cognition are called hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell;
they say the organs of action are speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the genitals. (26)

The ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose—these five are called the sense organs of cognition (*buddhīndriya*). Why are they called "sense organs of cognition"? Because these five are capable of grasping sound, form, and so forth, they are termed the sense organs of cognition. Speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ—these five are called the organs of action (*karmendriya*). Why are they called "organs of action"? Because these five perform the functions of speaking and so forth.

Therefore, the name "five organs of action" was established by the former teachers. An opponent asks: what are the respective functions (*svavṛtti*) of these ten organs? The organ of hearing is produced from the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*) and is of the same genus as the great element of space (*ākāśamahābhūta*); therefore, it perceives sound alone. The organ of touch is produced from the subtle element of tangibility (*sparśatanmātra*) and is of the same genus as the great element of air (*vāyumahābhūta*); therefore, it perceives tangibility alone.

The faculty of sight is produced from the subtle element of form (*rūpatanmātra*) and is of the same nature as the great element of fire; therefore, it perceives only form. The faculty of taste is produced from the subtle element of taste (*rasatanmātra*) and is of the same nature as the great element of water; therefore, it perceives only taste. The faculty of smell is produced from the subtle element of odor (*gandhatanmātra*) and is of the same nature as the great element of earth; therefore, it perceives only odor. In this way, there are five functions of the five organs of action.

The organ of speech, when conjoined with the faculty of cognition, is able to utter names, words, and syllables. The organ of the hands, when conjoined with the faculty of cognition, is well able to perform actions such as grasping and holding. The organ of the feet, when conjoined with the faculty of cognition, is able to walk upon paths that are level or uneven. The organ of generation, when conjoined with the faculty of cognition, bestows pleasure and produces offspring. The organ of excretion, when conjoined with the faculty of cognition, discharges feces and waste. For these purposes, the ten organs are enumerated. || 26 ||
The opponent asks: "What kind of faculty is the mind? The answer is given in the verse:
"In this context, the mind is of a dual nature; it is both the faculty of volition and a sense-faculty due to its common characteristics.
Its diversity arises from the specific transformations of the *guṇas* and from the difference in its objects. (27)

The mind (*manas*), which is the faculty of volition, is said to be of two kinds. The mind is a faculty that consists of both types, having volition as its essence. How so? When this mind is conjoined with a sense-faculty of cognition (*buddhīndriya*), it is designated as a sense-faculty of cognition; when it is conjoined with a faculty of action (*karmendriya*), it is designated as a faculty of action. Why? Because this mind conceives of the function of the sense-faculties of cognition.

And it also intends the activity of the organs of action (*karmendriya*). Just as a single person is sometimes called a laborer and sometimes a speaker, so too is the mind (*manas*). How is this mind called an organ? Because it possesses the same nature as the ten organs; for the ten organs arise from the *ahaṅkāra* of transformation (*vaikṛta*), and the mind as an organ is likewise. Furthermore, it shares the same function as the ten organs; whatever the ten organs perform, the mind as an organ performs in the same way.

Therefore, it receives the name "organ" (*indriya*). An opponent asks: "Are the functions of the organs distinct for each one, or is the function of the mental organ (*manas*) restricted [to a specific object] or not? It is replied: "That which is volition (*saṃkalpa*) is its very function. For example, a certain person, hearing that there is wealth or food in a certain place, says to himself: "I shall go there and obtain food and profit from it."

Volition (*saṃkalpa*) is the specific function of the mind (*manas*), which is itself a sense-organ (*indriya*). Because of their common origin and the similarity of their functions, as well as because of the specific regulation of volitional activity, it is designated as a sense-organ. Therefore, the sense-organs are indeed of eleven kinds. The opponent asks: "Who is the creator of these eleven sense-organs? If it is asked how such a doubt arises, it is due to the difference in the views of the teachers (*ācārya*). Some say they were created by the Person (*puruṣa*); others say they were created by the Lord (*īśvara*)."

Some say: "They are produced by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Such various positions are each inconsistent. Therefore, doubt has arisen in me. Regarding these objects of the senses, the eleven types of sense-faculties invariably function from that which possesses consciousness. How is this known? These eleven sense-faculties are capable of grasping the eleven respective objects. Since *pradhāna*, *mahat*, and *ahaṅkāra* are insentient, it is not logical for them to possess such capacity. As it is said in the *Lokāyata* treatise: "By whom were the swans made white and the parrots made green?"

"Mayūra, by whom you are painted, will provide for our livelihood. This is the statement of the Lokāyatika. Therefore, I now have this doubt: from what do the eleven sense-faculties (*indriya*) arise? It is said in reply: In this system, the *puruṣa* (Self) is not the agent, nor is Īśvara the agent. There is no distinct entity called "inherent nature" (*svabhāva*). Therefore, that which was mentioned by you—the *puruṣa* and so forth—does not produce the eleven sense-faculties. The opponent asks: "If that is so, then what factor is the producer? The answer is: "The diversity [of phenomena] arises from the specific transformation of the qualities (*guṇa-pariṇāma-viśeṣa*) and from external distinctions."

The three *guṇas* residing in the *ahaṅkāra* transform into the eleven organs by the power of the purpose of the *puruṣa*. What is this purpose of the *puruṣa*? These eleven external objects are numerous and diverse. If only a single organ were to function, it would not be capable of grasping all objects. Therefore, the eleven organs function, and each grasps its own specific object. Consequently, the eleven organs are distinct and manifold.

Now, if you say that what is insentient is not capable of producing many things, this is not tenable, because we observe the capacity for multiplicity in the insentient. For it will be stated in this treatise: "Just as the flow of milk, though insentient, occurs for the sake of the growth of the calf, so does the activity of the Pradhāna occur for the sake of the liberation of the Puruṣa. Thus.

Therefore, the three *guṇas*, being insentient, are capable of producing the eleven organs. An opponent says: "We know that the eleven organs are produced from *ahaṅkāra*. By whom was the distinct placement of these eleven organs made? The eye is situated high up and is capable of perceiving distant forms. The ear is situated on each side and hears distant sounds. The nose is located in one place and perceives odors by coming into contact with them."

The organ of taste, situated in the middle of the mouth, perceives the flavor that has arrived there. The sense of touch, located both internally and externally, knows all sensations of contact. Speech, situated in the middle of the mouth, articulates names, words, and syllables. The two hands, positioned on the left and right, are capable of grasping and holding. The two feet, situated in the lower parts of the body, move upward and downward. The sexual organ is situated in the private region for the purpose of avoiding the sight of others; it is capable of both emission and the production of pleasure.

The mind-faculty (*manas*), whose location is not fixed, performs the function of volition (*saṃkalpa*). By whom was the placement of these faculties established? Was it created by the Person (*puruṣa*)? Or by God (*īśvara*)? Or was it created by inherent nature (*svabhāva*) or some other additional cause? It is resolved: in this scripture, neither the Person nor God is said to be the cause. Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*) is the primary cause. Primordial Matter creates the three qualities (*guṇas*) and the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*).

And the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) functions by pursuing the purposes of the Puruṣa. By means of these three qualities (guṇas), the sense organs are established in their respective positions. Therefore it is said that their diversity arises from the specific transformations of the qualities and from external differences. For the sense organs, which function upon both proximate and remote objects, there are two purposes: the avoidance of what is to be abandoned and the preservation of the body. Regarding "the avoidance of what is to be abandoned": seeing at a distance and hearing at a distance serve for the avoidance of what is to be abandoned. Regarding "the preservation of the body": [this refers to the other functions].
The eight sense organs perceive the eight objects that have reached the location of the senses for the sake of increasing and maintaining their own bodies. 27.

The opponent asks: what function do these eleven faculties perform? The answer is given in verse: "The function of the five [sensory faculties] with respect to form and so forth is held to be mere observation;
while speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, and sexual pleasure are the functions of the other five. (28)

The function of the five sense organs (*buddhīndriya*) is merely the perception of objects such as form. The eye perceives form alone; this alone is the function of the eye. It perceives alone, but it does not resolve, retain, or grasp. The same applies to the remaining organs. Their respective functions consist solely in the illumination of their own particular objects. A sense organ is capable of illuminating an object; an action organ (*karmendriya*) is capable of grasping that which is to be enjoyed.

The function of the cognitive organs (*buddhīndriya*) has been explained. Now, the function of the active organs (*karmendriya*) is described: [beginning with] "speech" and so forth. Speech, that is, speaking, is the domain of the organ of speech (*vāgindriya*). Grasping is the domain of the hands. Moving about, that is, walking, is the domain of the feet. Pleasure and procreation are the domain of the generative organ (*upastha*). Excretion, that is, evacuation, is the domain of the anus. Thus, the functions of the active organs have been explained. (28)
Now, the functions of the Great Principle (mahat), the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), and the mind (manas) shall be explained.
The function of these three, according to their own specific characteristics, is unique to each;
however, the common function of the organs is the five vital airs, beginning with prāṇa. (29)

The function (*vṛtti*) of the intellect (*mahat*) is determination (*adhyavasāya*). The characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) is self-conceit (*abhimāna*); that very characteristic is the function of the ego. The characteristic of the mind (*manas*) is volition (*saṃkalpa*); that very characteristic is the function of the mind. Regarding the phrase "the uncommon [function] of the thirteen": the specific characteristics of the ten sense organs have been established separately; therefore, the uncommon function of these thirteen has been stated. The common function of the sense organs consists of the five vital airs (*prāṇa*), etc.

If it is said that there is no common function (*asāmānyavṛttitva*), then it is all the more understood that there must be a common function. An example of non-common function is a single woman belonging to each individual man. An example of common function is a single shared female servant belonging to many men. What is the common function of the sense organs? It is the fivefold vital airs: *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *udāna*, *vyāna*, and *samāna*. These five vital airs constitute the common function of all the sense organs; this is what is called the *prāṇavāyu*.

Its path is through the mouth and nose; its function is the grasping of external objects, namely: "I stand," "I go"—this indeed is its activity. Another asks: "Of which sense organ is this the activity? It is said: "This is the common activity of the thirteen organs. Just as a parrot in a cage moves the cage by its own movement, so too are the senses."

Due to the movement of the *prāṇa* wind, all thirteen sense organs move; therefore, it is the common function of those thirteen organs. Regarding the *apāna* wind: having seen an act of fear, one immediately retreats from it. If this wind is predominant, then the person becomes dejected. Regarding the *udāna* wind: by means of it, a person desires to climb a mountain, and thinks, "I am superior, no other is like me," and "I am capable of doing this."

If this *vāyu* is predominant, then a person becomes arrogant, thinking, "I am superior," "I am wealthy," and so forth; this is the function of *udāna*. The *vyāna* wind pervades the body and finally leaves the body. If this wind is predominant, then a person finds no pleasure except in himself. If this wind releases [the breath] little by little, then the limbs become like those of a corpse. If there is a complete release, then death occurs.

The *samāna* wind resides in the region of the heart; its function is the equalizing of food. This is its specific activity. If this wind is predominant, a person becomes greedy; he seeks wealth and seeks a companion. These are the five functions of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), performed by the thirteen organs. (29)
The specific and general functions of these thirteen faculties have been described. Now, their simultaneous and successive functions will be explained. He states this in an Āryā verse:
"The simultaneous function of four [faculties] and their successive function have been specified;
likewise, for the three [faculties], their function is preceded by that [perception]. (30)

Regarding whether the functions of the intellect (*buddhi*), ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), mind (*manas*), and the sense organ occur simultaneously or successively: in the perception of form, the Great Principle (*mahat*), ego-sense, mind, and the visual organ proceed together; they grasp a single object of cognition. Just as with the visual organ, so it is with the remaining organs; all four proceed simultaneously and grasp a single object of cognition equally.

The process of cognition occurs gradually, as follows: suppose someone walking on a path suddenly sees some elevated object and, at that moment, becomes uncertain, thinking, "Is this a post or a person? If he perceives the gathering of birds, or a bamboo ring, or a deer nearby, then he understands, "This is a post. If he perceives moving cloth, or contraction and extension [of limbs], then he understands, "This is a person."

Thus, the activity of the intellect (*buddhi*), ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), mind (*manas*), and the sense-faculties (*indriya*) occurs sequentially. Just as the eye performs the act of seeing, so too the other sense-faculties, such as the ear and so forth, should be understood as operating in succession. Regarding both seen and unseen objects, the activity of the triad [of intellect, ego, and mind] is preceded by the sense-faculties. Thus, it has been stated that in the case of the visible realm (*dṛṣṭadharme*), the sequential activity of the triad is based upon the sense-faculties. Now, the activity of the triad based upon the sense-faculties will also be explained with respect to the invisible realm (*adṛṣṭadharme*). As it is said in a verse: "At the time of the end of the age, people will come to exist as those who, through wicked views and conduct, revile the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha."
Being wicked, he will cause harm to his father, kinsmen, and friends;
having gone through the four miserable states of existence, he will lead others here as well.

Just as in the future, so too in the past, the sequential operation of the three dharmas has its basis in the faculty of hearing; thus, the threefold dharma proceeds preceded by the external sense organs. //30//

The opponent says: "If these thirteen instruments (*karaṇa*) are insentient and not presided over by either the *puruṣa* or the Lord (*īśvara*), how is it that they each individually grasp their own respective objects? He provides the answer in a verse: "Each attains its own function, which is caused by mutual intention;
the purpose of the *puruṣa* alone is the cause, for no instrument is set in motion by anyone else. (31)

"Thirteen [instruments] perform their own functions without another. It has been stated previously in this treatise that neither Īśvara nor Puruṣa is an agent. Therefore, the thirteen instruments perform their respective objects by themselves and not by means of another. For example, suppose a certain Brāhmaṇa student hears in a certain place that a Vedic teacher is teaching those who are studying as they please. He then resolves: "I shall certainly go there and study."

This very determination is formed by Mahat. Having perceived the intention of Ahaṅkāra, it thinks thus: "All the Brāhmaṇas are collecting whatever implements are available; I shall take everything and go. Once I have gone there, let my heart not falter. Having perceived the intention of Ahaṅkāra, Manas forms this resolve: "Which Veda shall I study first? Shall I study the Sāmaveda, or the Yajurveda?"

When the external sense organs thoroughly understand the mental intentions, the eye looks upon the path; the ear hears the words of others; the hand holds the water-pot; and the foot treads the road. Thus, each performs its own function individually, just as a leader of thieves issues a command: "Whether going out, entering, running, or standing still, you must all certainly obey me! And this entire band of thieves follows that command.

In the same way, these sense organs are also like this: the intellect (*buddhi*) is comparable to a king or a chief thief, while the remaining sense organs are comparable to a band of thieves. Through their knowledge of the intentions of the intellect, they each perform their own respective functions separately. An opponent asks: "Do these thirteen instruments (*karaṇa*) grasp the objects present before them for their own sake, or for the sake of another? The answer is given: "The purpose of the Puruṣa alone is the cause; an instrument is not set in motion by anything else. This meaning has been stated previously.

Since the purpose of the *puruṣa* is that which is to be accomplished, the *guṇas* create the sense organs (*indriyas*), which illuminate, bring about, and sustain the objects for the sake of the *puruṣa*. If it is asked by you: "How do these sense organs, being insentient, function? It is replied: There is no other Lord (*īśvara*) apart from these sense organs who, having entered into their midst, could preside over them for the sake of instructing their activity.

The Puruṣa, when conjoined with Prakṛti, thinks in this way merely for the sake of instigating activity: "For my sake of isolation (kaivalya), you must manifest yourself. For the sake of this purpose of the Puruṣa, the three Guṇas produce the sense organs; and they perform their respective functions under the influence of the Puruṣa's purpose. Therefore, apart from the purpose of the Puruṣa, there is no other separate motivator. 31.

The opponent asks: "Among the twenty-four principles (*tattvas*), how many are instruments (*karaṇas*)? The answer is given in an Āryā verse: "The instrument is of thirteen kinds; it performs the functions of grasping, maintaining, and manifesting.
And its object is tenfold: that which is to be grasped, maintained, and manifested. (32)

"The number of instruments (karaṇas) is thirteen. In this treatise, the instruments mentioned here and there are fixed at exactly thirteen: the five organs of cognition, the five organs of action, and the intellect (buddhi), ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), and mind (manas). What function do these thirteen perform? They are the causes of seizing, retaining, and illuminating. Their function is tenfold: the five objects such as sound and the five activities such as speaking; these ten are their respective effects.

[Furthermore], that effect is threefold: that which is to be brought forth (*āhārya*), that which is to be manifested (*prakāśya*), and that which is to be sustained (*dhārya*). Among these, [the first] is brought forth by the three [organs of action]; the five instruments of cognition manifest [the second]; and the five instruments of action sustain [the third]. It is for the sake of these three effects that the thirteen faculties are established. Therefore, it is said: "that which is to be brought forth, that which is to be sustained, and that which is to be manifested. (32)

The opponent asks: How many faculties grasp objects belonging to the three periods of time? And how many faculties grasp present objects? With a verse, he provides the answer: "The internal organ is threefold; the external is tenfold, known as the object of the [internal] triad.
The external functions in the present time; the internal organ functions in the three periods of time. (33)

"The internal organ is threefold" means that intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and mind (*manas*) are the three types. These are designated as the "internal organs" (*antaḥkaraṇa*). They are termed "internal" because they do not grasp external objects. They are called "organs" (*karaṇa*) because they are capable of serving as the means for accomplishing the purposes of the person (*puruṣārtha*). The ten external organs are the objects of these three; the ten external organs—the five sensory organs and the five organs of action—grasp external objects. Therefore, they are designated as "external organs" (*bāhyakaraṇa*).

"Objects of the triad" refers to the intellect (*buddhi*), ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), and mind (*manas*). The ten instruments (*karaṇa*) are held to be their objects. Just as a king employs his subjects, so too do these three internal organs cause the ten instruments to act. The external instrument perceives an object that is present; these ten kinds of instruments have as their domain objects existing in the present. How is this known? The faculty of hearing perceives sound only at the present time.

Because it is not perceived in the other two times, just as the sense of hearing [is not]. This applies likewise up to the sense of smell. The organ of speech articulates names, words, and phonemes belonging to the present; however, it does not articulate those that are past or future. Just as with the organ of speech, so it is with the remaining four [senses] as well. Internally, it grasps objects belonging to the three times. Thus, the intellect (*buddhi*), ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), and mind (*manas*)—these three types—grasp objects belonging to the three times.

The intellect (*buddhi*) perceives present objects such as jars and bowls; it also perceives the past, as when it is said, "In former times there was a king named Māndhātṛ"; and it also perceives the future, as when it is said, "The destruction of people will come to pass. Likewise, the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) also conceives of objects belonging to the three periods of time as "mine. Similarly, the organ of mind (*manas*) also forms volitions regarding objects of the three periods of time: it desires the future and remembers the past. Therefore, it is said that the internal [organ] perceives objects of the three periods of time. (33)

An opponent asks: How many sense organs grasp their objects with specific qualities (*saviśeṣa*), and how many grasp their objects without specific qualities (*nirviśeṣa*)? The answer is given in the *Āryā* verse:
"Among them, the five organs of cognition have as their objects both the specific and the non-specific;
speech has sound as its object, while the remaining [organs] also have fivefold objects. (34)

Among the thirteen [instruments], the organs of perception grasp objects that are both specific and non-specific. Among these thirteen instruments, the five organs of perception grasp objects that are both with and without specific qualities (*saviśeṣa* and *nirviśeṣa*). Those with specific qualities consist of the three *guṇas*; those without specific qualities possess only a single *guṇa*. For example, the five objects in heaven known as sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—these five objects are without specific qualities because they consist of an equal nature of *sattva*.

These five objects are devoid of *rajas* and *tamas*. In the human realm, the five objects are characterized by distinctions (*saviśeṣa*), being established through the conjunction of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Therefore, the sense organs of cognition (*buddhīndriya*) of the gods perceive objects that are without distinction (*nirviśeṣa*). However, the sense organs of cognition of humans perceive objects that possess the distinctions consisting of the forms of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Thus it is said: "The sense organs of cognition perceive both objects with and without distinction. Speech, moreover, has sound alone as its object.

The speech of gods and the speech of humans speak names, phrases, and syllables, which have sound alone as their object. For the remaining four [sense organs], all five objects are their domain. The hand-faculty consists of the five [objects] and grasps the fivefold objects. For example, the hand grasps a jar. As it is with the hand, so it is with the remaining faculties. Thus, the four faculties, being established upon the five objects, grasp the fivefold objects. (34)
Now, he states another characteristic of the sense organs in a verse:
"Since the intellect, together with the internal organ, penetrates every object, therefore the threefold instrument is the gatekeeper, while the remaining ones are the gates. (35)

"The intellect (*buddhi*), together with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), penetrates every object. Thus it is said that "the intellect is together with the internal organ" because the intellect is always joined with the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) and the mind-organ (*manas*). It penetrates the objects of the three worlds and the objects of the three times; therefore it is said that "it penetrates every object. Consequently, "the threefold instrument is the gatekeeper. This means that the threefold instrument, beginning with the intellect, makes [the Self] the lord of the gates.

If the threefold instrument consisting of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the others is properly joined with the visual faculty (*cakṣurindriya*), then that visual faculty illuminates form (*rūpa*), and not the remaining faculties. These three [instruments], through their integration with a single faculty, penetrate the objects of the three worlds and the objects of the three times. Therefore, it is said that these three [instruments] preside over the ten instruments; all the remaining faculties are merely "gates."

Namely, the five faculties of cognition and the five faculties of action. Because they follow the three instruments (*trikaraṇa*), they are either open or closed. If the triad [of instruments] is present in the eye, then the eye-door is open and it penetrates the object situated before it; however, the remaining doors are closed and do not perceive the object. Since they follow others, the doors are merely such and are not actually instruments.
Thus, the ten faculties, conjoined with the threefold instrument, penetrate all objects within the three worlds. (35)
Furthermore, the Noble One says:
"These specific qualities, which are like lamps and mutually distinct, having illuminated the entire purpose of the Puruṣa, present it to the intellect. (36)

"The instruments are like lamps" means: namely, the five organs of cognition (*jñānendriya*), the five organs of action (*karmendriya*), the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), and the mental organ (*manaindriya*). Just as a lamp situated in one place illuminates objects equally, so too do the instruments illuminate the objects of the three worlds. Therefore, it is said they are "like lamps. Following their respective qualities (*guṇa*), they are mutually distinct; that is, they possess different characteristics. The ear perceives sound, not form.

The eye perceives form, not sound; likewise, the nose perceives only odor, not taste. Among the organs of cognition (*jñānendriya*), each organ is restricted to its own specific object and is distinct from the others. Therefore, it is said that they are mutually distinct. The organs of action (*karmendriya*) are also like this: speech performs only the function of speaking; it does not perform the functions of the other [organs]. Likewise, the intellect (*buddhi*) performs only determination (*adhyavasāya*); the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) performs only self-conceit (*abhimāna*).

The mind (*manas*) performs only volition (*saṃkalpa*). For this reason also, it is said that they are mutually distinct. How is that distinction? Without abandoning the three *guṇas*, the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) proceeds in an uneven manner. Therefore, the ego-sense creates all the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*) and the sense organs (*indriyas*) in an uneven fashion. Having illuminated the objects of the three worlds, they present them to the intellect (*buddhi*) for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*). These twelve organs, having illuminated the objects of the world, present them all to the intellect.

Just as all the ministers in a kingdom collect the resources of the country and present them to the protector of the realm, so too do the objects of the senses deliver their impressions to the intellect through the twelve sense organs. Therefore, the intellect displays the objects to the person (puruṣa). Hence it is said that they present the purpose of the person to the intellect. || 36 ||
The opponent asks: Why is it that the sense organs, having manifested the objects, do not themselves present them to the Puruṣa? He provides the answer in an Āryā verse:
"Because the intellect accomplishes every experience for the Puruṣa, and it is that very intellect which distinguishes the subtle difference between Pradhāna and Puruṣa. (37)

Because the intellect (*buddhi*) accomplishes every experience for the person (*puruṣa*), the person’s enjoyment is not the same in all cases. Whether in the human realm, the divine realm, or the animal realm, the enjoyment of the ten objects—up to the enjoyment of the eight sovereign powers (*aṣṭaiśvarya*)—is not uniform. The ten external instruments, consisting of the organs of perception and the organs of action, having illuminated these objects, present them to the intellect; the intellect then accepts them in order to present them to the person.

By that means, the person (puruṣa) obtains experience. And by this cause, the intellect (buddhi) gradually makes the person a sovereign enjoyer of the bliss of mastery as desired, until discriminative wisdom (prajñā) arises. Furthermore, at a later time, it reveals the subtle distinction between primordial matter (pradhāna) and the person. This "later time" refers to the time of the manifestation of wisdom. People who have not practiced the conduct of discernment do not perceive this discrimination that primordial matter and the person are distinct.

Therefore, it is called "subtle. And that [subtlety] is the door to discrimination; thus, in the thirteenth [chapter], it is the intellect (*buddhi*) alone that reveals the Puruṣa. What is the characteristic of this vision? It is as follows: the vision is that the *pradhāna* and the Puruṣa are distinct; the three *guṇas* are distinct; the intellect is distinct; the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) is distinct; the eleven organs are distinct; the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) are distinct; the five gross elements (*mahābhūta*) are distinct; and the body is distinct. This is the vision.

The cognition of such distinctions produces knowledge in the Puruṣa; from that, the Puruṣa attains liberation, as was stated previously: "One who knows the twenty-five principles, in whatever stage of life he may dwell—whether he has matted hair, a shaven head, or a topknot—he is liberated; of this there is no doubt. Therefore, in reality, the intellect alone is the instrument of the Puruṣa. (37)
The opponent says: It was stated previously in the Āryā that the senses grasp both specific and non-specific objects. What are those specific and non-specific [objects]? The Āryā gives the answer:
"The subtle elements (tanmātras) are the non-specific; from these five, the five gross elements arise.
These are known as the specific, being calm, terrible, and delusive. (38)

"The five *tanmātras* are the non-specific (*aviśeṣa*). You have asked: "What are the specific (*viśeṣa*) and the non-specific? This shall now be explained. From the *ahaṅkāra*, the five subtle *tanmātras* arise; they are tranquil, characterized by *sattva*, and these alone are the objects of the gods and are non-specific, because for the gods there is an absence of sorrow and delusion. From those [non-specific *tanmātras*] arise the five gross elements (*mahābhūtas*). The objects consisting of the elements are the specific. From the *tanmātra* of sound, space (*ākāśa*) arises.

...until from the subtle element of smell (*gandhatanmātra*), earth is produced. These five elements possess specific qualities (*saviśeṣa*). What are the characteristics of these specific qualities? They are tranquil (*śānta*), terrible (*ghora*), and delusive (*mūḍha*). Those five great elements (*pañcamahābhūta*) are the objects of human experience. What are the three characteristics of the great element of space (*ākāśamahābhūta*)? For example, just as some wealthy man, having entered an inner chamber, enjoys the pleasures of the five senses; and at another time, having ascended a lofty palace, he beholds the great element of space from afar.

Because one experiences pleasure through that space, it is "peaceful" (*śānta*). Alternatively, when one is situated in a lofty palace and is touched by the cool wind of the sky, then space is a producer of suffering. Or again, someone traveling on a great road sees only the sky and does not see a collection of villages; and since there is no place of rest, it then becomes a producer of delusion (*moha*). The same applies to the remaining great elements (*mahābhūta*).

Thus, for the gods, the five subtle elements (tanmātras) are objects that are exclusively tranquil; therefore, they are without distinction (aviśeṣa). For humans, the objects are the gross elements (mahābhūtas). And since the gross elements possess the three qualities (guṇas), they are with distinction (saviśeṣa). || 38 ||

The opponent says: The specific characteristics have been explained according to their classification. Are these the only specific characteristics, or are there other specific characteristics as well? It is replied: There are indeed other specific characteristics. As it has been said: "Subtle, those born of mother and father, and together with the abundant—thus the specific characteristics are of three kinds.
Among them, the subtle ones are constant; those born of mother and father cease. (39)

There are three kinds of distinctions: the subtle, those born of parents, and the abundant. In the beginning, all things in the three worlds arise as subtle bodies consisting solely of the *tanmātras*. Those subtle bodies enter the womb. The union of semen and blood causes the subtle body to grow. The sixfold essences of food and drink, once nourished, sustain the accumulation and growth of the gross body. The mother and the son are connected through the channels of food and drink.

Therefore, the gross body (*sthūla-śarīra*) is nourished and grows. Just as a tree grows by being moistened because its roots are connected to a source of water, so too this essence of food and drink, having entered within through its path of circulation, causes the gross body to grow. Whatever is the measure of the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*), such is the measure of the gross body as well. The subtle body is called "internal," while the gross body is called "external."

In this subtle body, the human characteristics—the hands, feet, head, mouth, belly, and back—become complete. As the great seers declare in the four Vedas: "The gross body has six supports. Blood, flesh, and sinews are the threefold elements born of the mother; semen, marrow, and bones are the threefold elements born of the father. These are the six supports of the body. By means of the external gross body, the internal subtle body is nourished and developed.

When this internal subtle body, which has been nourished by the gross body, emerges from the womb at the time of birth, the external five great elements (pañcamahābhūta) become its places of habitation. Just as for a prince, others construct a house with various halls and palaces, saying, "This place is fit for recreation, this place is fit for eating, and this place is fit for sleeping."

In the same way, Pradhāna also creates the five great elements (mahābhūtas) in order to provide a locus and instruments for the subtle and gross bodies. It creates the great element of space (ākāśa) for providing accommodation; the great element of earth (pṛthivī) for movement; the great element of water (ap) for purification; the great element of fire (tejas) for the digestion of food; and the great element of air (vāyu) for distribution. Thus, there are three kinds of specific effects: the subtle [elements], those born of mother and father [the gross elements], and those consisting of the peaceful, the terrible, and the deluded [the sense objects].

These three others are called *viśeṣas* (distinctive evolutes). Another asks: "Among these three *viśeṣas*, how many are eternal and how many are non-eternal? He replies: "Among the three, the subtle ones are constant; the rest cease. Among these three, the five *tanmātras* are observed as the subtle *viśeṣas*. They are the progenitors of the first body and are constant. When the gross body ceases, and if the subtle body is joined with demerit (*adharma*), it then assumes four types of births.

The four-footed, the winged, the serpent, and the animal—these are the forms it assumes if it is joined with merit (*dharma*). Then it takes up four types of births: as Brahmā, a god, a progenitor (*prajāpati*), or a human. Thus, the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*), being constant, transmigrates through the eight stations until knowledge and detachment (*jñāna-vairāgya*) have arisen. If knowledge and detachment have arisen, then, released from this body, it is liberated. Therefore it is said that the specific [qualities] of the subtle body are eternal.

The remaining gross particulars, as they cease to exist, are called impermanent. At the time of death, the subtle body abandons the gross body. This gross body—born of mother and father—is either devoured by birds, or it decays and putrefies, or it is consumed by fire. The subtle body of the deluded one wanders through the cycle of worldly existence. 39.

The opponent says: You have stated that the body born of mother and father ceases [to exist]. But what, then, is it that transmigrates in *saṃsāra*? With the following verse, the Noble One provides the answer:

"The *liṅga* (the subtle body), which has arisen previously, is unattached, constant, beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*) and ending with the subtle elements; devoid of enjoyment, it transmigrates, being perfumed by dispositions (*bhāva*). (40)

"The previously arisen body is unattached. In the past, the *pradhāna* (primordial matter), being in motion, created the world. First, the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*) was born. From *pradhāna*, the intellect (*buddhi*) was born; from the intellect, the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) was born; and from the ego, the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) were born. These seven are called the subtle body. What is the characteristic of the subtle body? It is similar in form to Brahman. After experiencing sense objects, one subsequently attains liberation through this body.

"Unattached," as it has been said by the Teachers: "Even though this subtle body (sūkṣmaśarīra) resides within the states of animals, humans, and gods, it cannot be obstructed by mountains, stones, walls, and the like, because of its subtlety. Nor is it subject to transformation. As long as higher wisdom (prajñā) does not arise, it is never separated from it; this is declared to be constant. It is called the Great One (mahat), egoism (ahaṅkāra), and the five subtle elements (pañcatanmātra). By how many principles (tattvas) is this body constituted?

By means of the seven subtle principles (*sūkṣmatattva*) up to the sixteen gross principles (*sthūlatattva*), what does this body do? It transmigrates; it experiences objects that are beyond the senses. That subtle body, conjoined with the eleven organs, having entered into four types of births, transmigrates through the three worlds. Regarding "experiencing objects that are beyond the senses": if it were not conjoined with the eleven organs, and if it were devoid of the gross body born of mother and father, then it would lack the capacity for the experience of sense objects.

"The subtle body is perfumed by dispositions (*bhāva*). There are three kinds of dispositions belonging to the subtle body; it is "perfumed" by these dispositions. These three dispositions will be explained later: innate disposition (*sāṃsiddhika-bhāva*), natural disposition (*prākṛtika-bhāva*), and acquired disposition (*vaikṛta-bhāva*). Thus, the dispositions are of three kinds. The subtle body is perfumed by these three dispositions. It is called "the mark" (*liṅga*) because it is not perceived by the ignoble. That subtle body migrates through the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). (40)

The opponent says: "These thirteen faculties are sufficient for wandering in saṃsāra; what is the use of a false subtle body (mithyā-sūkṣma-śarīra)? The Noble One gives the reply: "Just as a painting cannot exist without a support, and just as there is no shadow without a post or other such object, so too the subtle body (liṅga) does not remain without its specific constituents (aviśeṣas); it cannot exist without a support. (41)

Just as a painting does not exist without a wall, nor does a shadow exist without a post or similar object; in this world, the two properties of the support (*ādhāra*) and the supported (*ādheya*) are seen to be conjoined, never separated. For example, the form of a painting has the wall as its substratum; it does not remain apart from the wall. Therefore, the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*), consisting of thirteen components, cannot exist apart from [the gross body]. Furthermore, without a post, a shadow would be without support; in the absence of fire, there is no light.

In the absence of water, there is no coolness; in the absence of air, there is no touch; without space, the modes of movement (īryāpatha) are not accomplished. Likewise, without the subtle body, the gross body remains without support and ceases to exist. Therefore it is said: "If [the self] were separated from the body composed of the five subtle elements, the thirteenfold [organ-complex] would remain without support. (41)

The opponent asks: For what purpose does this subtle body wander through the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) together with the thirteenfold [group]? With a verse, he provides the answer: "This subtle body (liṅga) exists like an actor, due to the power of Nature (prakṛti), through the connection between causes and their effects, for the sake of the Puruṣa’s purpose. (42)

"Caused by the purpose of the *puruṣa*. Because the purpose of the *puruṣa* must be accomplished, the *pradhāna* undergoes transformation. The purpose of the *puruṣa* is twofold: the objective of perceiving sound and the other sense-objects, and the final one, which is the discernment of the difference between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa*. In states such as those of Brahmā, *puruṣas* become joined with the objects of sound and the rest; having been so joined, they are subsequently liberated. Therefore, the *pradhāna* transforms itself into the subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīra*). For what reason does this subtle body transmigrate? It is due to the cause consisting of the "efficient cause" (*nimitta*) and the "caused effect" (*naimittika*).
The sign (nimitta) consists of eight types, beginning with dharma, which will be explained later. The Noble One himself says:
"By means of dharma there is upward movement; by means of adharma there is downward movement.
Through knowledge there is liberation (apavarga), and from its opposite, bondage is held to occur."

Furthermore, by what cause do these signs (*nimitta*) and their corresponding effects (*naimittika*) succeed? It is through the power of the sovereign capacity of *prakṛti*. Just as a certain provincial governor (*rāṣṭrapāla*) performs his duties within his own kingdom according to its resources, so too does *pradhāna* (primordial matter) effect the creation of gods, humans, animals, and so forth. Therefore it is said: "The subtle body (*liṅga*) proceeds like an actor. Just as an actor is seen at one time in the form of a god, and at another time in the form of a king.

Sometimes it is seen in various and distinct forms, such as those of a nāga or a piśāca. Likewise, the subtle body (sūkṣma-śarīra), though composed of thirteen constituents, sometimes enters the womb of an elephant or a horse and transforms into the nature of an elephant or a horse; sometimes it enters the womb of a human or a deity and transforms into the nature of a human or a deity. Therefore it is said: "The subtle body (liṅga) proceeds like an actor, according to the pervasive power of primordial nature (prakṛti). || 42 ||

The opponent says: It was stated previously that the thirteen faculties, being colored by the three kinds of dispositions (*bhāva*), transmigrate in *saṃsāra*. What are those three kinds of dispositions? He provides the answer in an Āryā verse: "The dispositions are innate (*sāṃsiddhika*), natural (*prākṛtika*), and acquired (*vaikṛta*), such as virtue (*dharma*) and the rest;
they are observed to reside in the instruments (*karaṇa*) and to reside in the effects (*kārya*), such as the embryo (*kalala*) and so forth. (43)

There are three types of dispositions (*bhāva*): those that are innate (*sāṃsiddhika*), those that are natural (*prākṛtika*), and those that are acquired (*vaikṛta*). All dispositions are designated as *bhāva* and are of these three kinds: innate, natural, and acquired. The innate are, for example, the four qualities that were born together with the sage Kapila at the beginning: virtue (*dharma*), knowledge (*jñāna*), dispassion (*virāga*), and sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). These fourfold qualities are innate; therefore, these four qualities reside in the innate disposition. What are the natural ones? Regarding "natural": [they are those produced by the primary elements].

As it is stated in the Veda: "In ancient times, four sons were born to Brahmā, named Sankara, Sanandana, Sanātana, and Sanatkumāra. When these four sons—whose faculties and functions were fully developed and who possessed bodies—reached their sixteenth year, four states known as virtue (dharma), knowledge (jñāna), dispassion (virāga), and sovereignty (aiśvarya) spontaneously manifested, like the sudden discovery and acquisition of a treasure. These four states were not obtained through external causes; therefore, they are called 'natural' (prākṛtika)."

Regarding the phrase "transformed states" (*vaikṛtā bhāvāḥ*): "transformation" (*vikṛti*) refers to the form of the Teacher (*ācāryamūrti*). On account of the Teacher’s form as a cause, disciples approach him with reverence and devotion; having approached and heard [his teaching], they obtain knowledge. From knowledge they obtain dispassion (*vairāgya*); from dispassion they obtain merit (*dharma*); and from merit they obtain the eightfold sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). These four qualities of the disciple are called "transformed" because they are acquired through the form of the Teacher.

The internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*), perfumed by these four qualities, transmigrates within *saṃsāra*. These four qualities, together with their opposites, are eightfold. Upon what do these eight factors depend? The answer is stated: "The visible [qualities] depend upon the internal organ, while the subtle ones, such as the embryo (*kalala*) and so forth, depend upon the subtle body. That which is the internal organ begins with the Great Principle; it is endowed with the eight states including the Great Principle itself. Four of them depend upon the Great Principle, as was previously stated: "Intellection (*buddhi*) is determination (*adhyavasāya*); it consists of virtue (*dharma*), knowledge (*jñāna*), dispassion (*virāga*), and power (*aiśvarya*)."
"This form is characterized by *sattva*; that which is contrary to it is characterized by *tamas*.

Thus, these eightfold types of perfected beings (*siddhas*) reside within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). These eight states have been perceived by noble persons with their divine vision; therefore, it is said, "they have been seen. Furthermore, those residing in the subtle state are the *kalala* and so forth. The eightfold bodies are known as *kalala*, *budbuda*, *peśī*, *ghana*, *māṃsa*, *garbha*, *kumāra*, *yauvana*, and *sthāvira*. These eight types attain growth through the four kinds of food-essence (*annarasa*). The six flavors derived from the mother nourish the four bodies.

The embryonic body grows from the essence of milk; the childhood body grows from the drinking of breast milk; and the essence resulting from the remaining food nourishes the final two bodies. This eightfold body is perfected by depending upon the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*). These sixteen categories (*padārtha*) perfume the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and the subtle body migrates through the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). (43)

The opponent says: It was previously stated that the *liṅga* (the subtle body) proceeds like an actor due to the relationship between cause and effect (*nimitta-naimittika*). In that regard, what is the cause and what is the effect? He provides the answer: "By virtue of *dharma* there is upward movement; by virtue of *adharma* there is downward movement.
Through knowledge comes liberation (*apavarga*); from its opposite, bondage is held to occur. (44)

If a person in the world practices the dharma of restraints (*yama*), observances (*niyama*), and so forth, by that dharma, at the time of taking birth, the subtle body ascends and is born in eight locations: the state of a Brāhmaṇa, of Prajāpati, of Indra, of Gandharva, of Yakṣa, of Rākṣasa, of Yama, and of Piśāca; thus one obtains birth in these eight locations. If, however, one performs unrighteousness (*adharma*) which is the opposite of those ten kinds of dharma, at the time of taking birth, [the subtle body] descends and is born in five locations.

Through unrighteousness (*adharma*), one is born among the five states of existence: quadrupeds, birds, reptiles, animals, and stationary beings. Liberation (*apavarga*) results from knowledge and spiritual agitation (*udvega*). Through the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*), one attains knowledge; through knowledge, one attains dispassion (*vairāgya*); and through dispassion, one abandons the subtle body. Liberation is defined as the absolute isolation (*kaivalya*) of the Puruṣa. Conversely, when this is absent, there is bondage (*bandha*). Ignorance (*ajñāna*) is the opposite of knowledge.

Just as a person says, "I am to be pitied," "I am dear," or "This is dear to me"—it is from egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) alone that one conceives "I am. This is called ignorance (*ajñāna*). This ignorance binds one's own body. By means of it, one exists among humans, gods, and animals. Bondage is threefold: bondage by nature (*prakṛti-bandha*), bondage by transformation (*vikṛti-bandha*), and bondage by sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā-bandha*). These three will be explained later. Therefore, it was said: "the cause and the effect. Dharma is declared to be the cause.

Upward movement is the effect; unrighteousness (*adharma*) is the cause. Downward movement is the effect; ignorance (*ajñāna*) and lack of aversion (*anudvega*) are the causes. Liberation (*apavarga*) is the effect; knowledge (*jñāna*) and aversion (*udvega*) are the causes. Bondage (*bandha*) is the effect; ignorance and lack of aversion are the causes. Thus, four causes and four effects have been stated. 44.

Furthermore, there are four signs and four effects of those signs; these he will now explain: "From dispassion comes dissolution into nature; from passion, characterized by activity (rajas), comes worldly existence; from attachment comes worldly existence; from power comes non-obstruction; from its opposite comes the reverse. (45)

"From dispassion comes dissolution into primordial nature (*prakṛtilaya*). For example, suppose a certain Brahmin has renounced the world and, while studying the path, restrains his eleven sense organs; he avoids the eleven objects of the senses from afar and maintains the tenfold duties such as restraint (*yama*) and observance (*niyama*). At that time, he experiences a sense of revulsion (*udvega*). From revulsion comes dispassion (*vairāgya*). However, because he lacks knowledge of the twenty-five principles (*tattva*), there is no liberation (*apavarga*) for him. When he dies, he merely dissolves into the eight forms of primordial nature.

The eight constituent natures (*prakṛti*) are as follows: from primordial nature (*prakṛti*) arise intellect (*buddhi*), ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*), and the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*). Abiding within these eight natures, one who has not attained liberation imagines himself to be liberated. Subsequently, at the time of transmigration, he again produces a gross body within the three worlds. Therefore it is said: "Through dispassion, there is dissolution into nature (*prakṛtilaya*). This is called the "bondage of nature" (*prakṛtibandha*). Transmigration occurs through passionate attachment (*rāga*); thus, attachment is of the quality of passion (*rājasa*). For example, someone might think: [text continues]

"I am practicing great charity, performing great sacrifices as a service to the gods, drinking the soma juice, and I shall experience happiness in the next world"—through this passion for sovereignty (*rāja-rāga*), one takes birth in the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) from the station of Brahmā down to the animal species. This is called "bondage by sacrificial fees" (*dakṣiṇā-bandha*). Regarding "unimpededness through sovereignty": sovereignty consists of the eightfold powers such as *aṇimā* (minuteness) and *laghimā* (lightness), which belong to the class of *sattva*. By means of this sovereignty, one reaches the station of Brahmā and others, where there is freedom from the eight kinds of impediments.

The eight forms of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) attained through the method of faith (*imanaya*) are called "bondage through modification" (*vikṛtibandha*) because of their connection with the intellect (*buddhi*). From the opposite of that, there is "obstruction" (*vighāta*). That which is contrary to sovereignty is non-sovereignty (*anaiśvarya*); by means of non-sovereignty, there is obstruction everywhere. This obstruction is also "bondage through modification," because it possesses the quality of darkness (*tāmasa*). In this verse, four causes (*nimitta*) and their effects (*naimittika*) are stated: detachment (*vairāgya*) is the cause; dissolution into primordial nature (*prakṛtilaya*) is the effect. Passion belonging to the quality of activity (*rājasa-rāga*) is the cause.

Saṃsāra is the effect; sovereignty is the cause. Non-obstruction is the effect; lack of sovereignty is the cause. Obstruction is the effect. Thus, these sixteen creations—eight causes and eight effects—have been described. || 45 ||
The opponent asks: "Of what nature are these sixteen creations consisting of causes and their effects? He provides the answer in an Āryā verse:
"This is the creation of the intellect (*pratyayasarga*), known as error, incapacity, contentment, and attainment.
Through the mutual suppression of the inequality of the *guṇas*, its subdivisions number fifty. (46)

"Creation consists of the nature of the intellect as its cause. Regarding "creation": it is either the sixteenfold [set] or the eightfold set of derivative (naimittika) creations. If it is sixteenfold, then the eight causes and the eight derivatives consist of the intellect. Or, according to the view that it is eightfold, the eight derivative creations are what is termed "creation," and the eight causes consist of that [intellect]. Therefore it is said: "The sixteenfold creation consists of the nature of the intellect as its cause," just as previously stated by the Ācārya.

"Intellect (*buddhi*) is determination; its forms are virtue, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty—this is the *sāttvika* form; the *tāmasa* is the opposite of this. Thus it is said. "Error, incapacity, contentment, and attainment"—these sixteen varieties of manifestation are divided into four groups: error, incapacity, contentment, and attainment. For example, a certain Brāhmaṇa, together with four disciples, returned to his own home from a great protector of the realm.

While traveling on the road before sunrise, one of his disciples then said to the teacher: "Teacher, I see some object in the middle of the path; I do not know whether it is a post or a person. Thus, a doubt regarding the post arose in this disciple. The teacher said to a second disciple: "Go, examine and look closely—whether it is a person or a post. At the teacher's word, he looked from a distance.

He was not able to go near him. Then he said to the teacher, "Teacher, I am unable to go near him. This was the incapacity of the second man. Then he spoke to the third disciple: "Examine it thoroughly and determine what this is. Having examined it, he said to the teacher, "Teacher, what is the purpose of this examination? When the sun has risen, a great caravan leader will appear."

"We shall follow," he said; thus, even though this third man had not yet distinguished between the post and the person, satisfaction arose within him. Then he said to the fourth disciple, "Go and look at it. Because his faculty of sight was pure, this man saw the coil of cane and rope, and above it, a flock of birds. Having gone there, he touched its base. Returning, he said to the teacher, "Teacher, this is a post. Indeed, this fourth man attained perfection.

Therefore, the sixteen types of creation are divided into four groups. This is due to the consideration of the inequality of the *guṇas*. The *guṇas* are threefold: *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. These three are mutually opposed. If *sattva* is predominant, it overcomes *rajas* and *tamas*, just as the light of the sun overcomes the stars, fire, and so forth. The same applies when *rajas* is predominant. If one reflects upon the inequality of the three *guṇas* and so forth, then the fifty-fold creations of the intellect (*buddhi*) are distinguished. || 46 ||
Now he will describe the fifty divisions:
there are five varieties of error (viparyaya), and incapacity (aśakti) arises from the impairment of the organs;
contentment (tuṣṭi) has twenty-eight varieties, and accomplishment (siddhi) is ninefold and eightfold. (47)

There are five varieties of error (viparyaya). Error was previously mentioned; now its five varieties are stated: darkness (tamas), delusion (moha), great delusion (mahāmoha), gloom (tāmisra), and utter darkness (andhatāmisra). || 47 ||
Now, without yet describing the incapacities (*aśakti*), he first elucidates the five varieties of error (*viparyaya*):
"The division of *tamas* is eightfold; that of *moha* is likewise; *mahāmoha* is tenfold;
*tāmisra* is eighteenfold; and so too is *andhatāmisra*. (48)

Thus, the eight divisions of *tamas* have been stated. If a person, through ignorance, becomes detached [from the world] and merges into the eight primordial natures (*prakṛtis*)—namely, *pradhāna*, *buddhi*, *ahaṅkāra*, and the five *tanmātras*—this person, though not having attained liberation, considers himself to have attained it. This is because he has not perceived the eightfold bondage. Therefore, it is said that the eightfold vision is *tamas*. *Tamas* is another name for *avidyā*. Regarding "the eight [divisions] of delusion" (*moha*): the eightfold sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) was previously mentioned.

Therein, gods and others who are bound by the arising of passion do not attain liberation. Because they wander through *saṃsāra* due to attachment to power (*aiśvarya*), the eightfold division of delusion (*moha*) has been described. The first eight are called the "bond of primordial nature" (*prakṛti-bandha*). The latter eight are called the "bond of transformation" (*vikṛti-bandha*). Regarding "the ten of great delusion" (*mahāmoha*): the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), characterized by the quality of goodness (*sattva*), are the objects of the gods. These five objects, when conjoined with the five gross elements, possess the characteristics of the three qualities (*triguṇa*).

Regarding these ten objects, beings such as Brahmās, humans, and animals—having abandoned these—find no other superior object outside of them; thus, they become bound by the arising of passion. Through that attachment, they generally lack knowledge and the dharma of liberation; being addicted to sense-objects, they do not seek liberation. Therefore, this is named "Great Delusion" (mahāmoha). Regarding "the eighteen [types] of darkness" (tāmisra): when the eightfold sovereignty does not prevail over the tenfold objects, a poor person reflects as follows:

"I am poor; all my sovereignty and sense-objects have perished"—for one who forms such a mental disposition (*vṛtti*), eighteen types of suffering arise. These sufferings are called *tāmisra*. There are likewise eighteen for *andhatāmisra*, consisting as previously stated of the eightfold sovereignty and the tenfold objects of the senses. Endowed with these eighteen, at the very moment of death, a person reflects in this manner:

"I shall renounce the eightfold sovereignty and the ten objects of the senses; the wardens of hell will bind me and lead me to the abode of King Yama. Through this thought, suffering arises, and one is no longer capable of hearing the Sāṅkhya doctrine. Therefore, this [suffering] is called *andhatāmisra*. Thus, there are sixty-two varieties of the five types beginning with *tamas*. (48)
Now he states the divisions of incapacity (*aśakti*):
"Incapacity is declared to consist of the eleven defects of the organs together with the defects of the intellect;
the seventeen defects of the intellect arise from the inversion of contentment (*tuṣṭi*) and attainment (*siddhi*). (49)

The eleven impairments of the faculties (*indriyavadha*) are: deafness, blindness, loss of smell, impairment of the tongue, leprosy, insanity, muteness, crookedness, lameness, sterility, and constipation (*udāvarta*). These are the eleven impairments of the faculties. How is it said that these constitute "incapacity"? Because of the inability to hear and so forth, one is incapable of attaining liberation. For example, a deaf man—even if afflicted by other diseases—might say to a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*): "I am suffering; what should I do?"

The spiritual friend said, "Embrace the knowledge of Sāṅkhya; having reached the end of suffering and the destruction of suffering, you will attain liberation. He replied, "I am not capable of accepting the knowledge of Sāṅkhya; I will not listen to the words of my teacher. Without hearing the words of the teacher, how could knowledge arise? Just as one who is deaf, so too those who are blind and others, due to the impairment of their faculties, are unable to acquire knowledge, nor are they able to attain liberation.
The impairments of the intellect (*buddhi*) are declared to be incapacity. There are seventeen such impairments of the intellect, as will be explained later.
This concludes the middle section of the *Suvarṇasaptatiśāstra*.
Now begins the final section of the *Suvarṇasaptatiśāstra*.

"From the reversal of contentment and attainment. This refers to the reversal of the nine types of contentment and the eight types of attainment. The reversal of these seventeen is designated as the "destruction of the intellect" (*buddhi-vadha*). These eleven destructions of the faculties (*indriya-vadha*) and seventeen destructions of the intellect constitute the twenty-eight varieties of incapacity (*aśakti*). (49)
How are there nine varieties of contentment? Explaining this in Āryā meter, he says:
"The four internal [contentments] are named Nature (prakṛti), Means (upādāna), Time (kāla), and Fortune (bhāgya);
the five external [contentments] arise from the cessation of objects; thus nine contentments have been declared. (50)

The four internal satisfactions are those consisting of nature (*prakṛti*), acquisition (*upādāna*), time (*kāla*), and fortune (*bhāgya*). "Internal" refers to those four satisfactions that proceed with reference to the intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and mind (*manas*). These are: satisfaction through nature, satisfaction through the search for acquisition, satisfaction through time, and satisfaction through the attainment of fortune. To illustrate these four satisfactions, the following example is given: just as Brahmins, having abandoned their homes, go forth into the religious life.

In that regard, a certain person asks: "Having realized what have you gone forth? He replies: "I know the Pradhāna, the true cause of these three worlds; therefore I have gone forth. That Brāhmaṇa knows only that it is the Pradhāna which is the cause; he does not know whether it is eternal or non-eternal, conscious or unconscious, with qualities (saguṇa) or without qualities (nirguṇa), all-pervading (vyāpin) or non-pervading. However, he knows that "it exists" and that it is the "cause."

From this, contentment arises; yet he is not liberated. This contentment is born of primordial nature (*prakṛti*). Then he asks the second Brahmin: "Knowing what have you gone forth? He replies: "I know that *pradhāna* is the cause of the world, and I have known that the means of liberation is *upādāna*. Even though there is the knowledge that *pradhāna* is the true cause, if *upādāna* does not exist, liberation is not accomplished. Therefore, I accept *upādāna*."

*Upādāna* (appropriation) is the imitation of the mode of conduct practiced by all those who have gone forth (*pravrajita*). That equipment (*upakaraṇa*) is fourfold: the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*), the water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*), the ochre robe (*kaṣāya*), and auspicious marks (*maṅgala*). The ash-container (*bhasmakośikā*), the *rudrākṣa* bead, the body encircled by three threads (*tritantu*), the recitation of mantras, and the placing of *kuśa* grass and creepers upon the topknot (*jaṭāgra*)—these five implements of training and conduct are called "auspicious" (*maṅgala*) because they remove impurity. Together with the three previously established [items], there are eight implements.

"Thinking, 'I shall obtain liberation from these,' I have gone forth as a renunciant"—this is the second contentment called "acquisition. Through this contentment, one does not obtain liberation; one merely knows that *pradhāna* is the cause, and nothing more. Then he asks the third Brahmin: "Knowing what have you gone forth? He replies: "What are *pradhāna* and the four types of acquisition capable of doing?"

"I know that even without material acquisition (*upādāna*) or time (*kāla*), I shall attain liberation; therefore, I desire to go forth into the religious life. This is the third [type of contentment], which is not liberated. Why? Because of the lack of knowledge regarding the twenty-five principles (*padārtha*). This is the third contentment, known as "contentment with time" (*kālatuṣṭi*). Then he asks the fourth Brahmin: "Knowing what have you gone forth? He replies: "What is capable of accomplishing anything—whether primordial matter (*pradhāna*), material acquisition, or time—if one is devoid of the attainment of fortune (*bhāgya*)?"

"I have realized that through the attainment of good fortune (bhāgya) I shall obtain liberation; therefore, I have renounced the world. Even this fourth [type of contentment] does not lead to liberation, because of the absence of true knowledge. This is the fourth contentment, known as "contentment with the attainment of good fortune" (bhāgyalābhatuṣṭi). These four contentments are established as occasional (naimittika). Including the five external contentments arising from the cessation of the objects of the senses, there are nine in total. The external contentments are of five kinds.

Because of the cessation of the five sense-objects from afar—having seen the defects of acquisition, preservation, loss, lack of contentment, and violence—just as a certain man, seeing five Brahmin mendicants, approaches them one by one and asks; first he asks the first Brahmin: "Knowing what have you gone forth? He replies: "In the world there are five sense-objects."

The means for acquiring sense-objects are as follows: whether it be agriculture, or cattle-rearing, or service to a king, or trade—all of these are difficult to practice. Setting aside those four modes of livelihood, one might resort to theft; yet even this mode of acquiring sense-objects is invariably difficult to practice because it involves the infliction of suffering upon oneself and others. Having seen that these modes of livelihood are difficult, I desire to go forth into homelessness. This fifth Brahmin is not liberated, because he does not know reality.

Then he asks the second Brahmin: "Knowing what have you gone forth? He replies: "I know that the five sense-objects are obtained through seeking, as previously described by means such as agriculture and so forth. Once the sense-objects are obtained, their protection is difficult. Why? Because the five household activities are mutually contradictory. By protecting the sense-objects, both oneself and others are harmed. Seeing the suffering inherent in protection, I have desisted from sense-objects and gone forth."

"For this sixth one also there is no liberation, because he does not know reality. Then he asks the third: "Knowing what have you gone forth? He replies: "I am capable of seeking and acquiring that which has not been acquired; having acquired it, I protect it for the sake of its imperishability. These five objects of sense naturally diminish through one's own enjoyment. At the time of their exhaustion, great suffering arises. Because I perceive the fault in these exhausted objects, I desire the life of a renunciant. Thus he spoke.

This man also does not attain liberation because he does not know reality. Then he asks the fourth question: "Knowing what have you gone forth? He replies: "I am capable of seeking that which I have not yet obtained; having acquired it, I protect it; and even when it is exhausted, I acquire it again. If this is so, why have I gone forth? My five sense-faculties are never satisfied, for they seek ever more excellent things. I perceive the fault in these sense-faculties; therefore, I desire the life of a renunciant."

"Thus, even for this eighth [type], there is no liberation, because of their lack of knowledge of reality (*atattvajñatva*). Then he asks about the fifth: 'Knowing what have you gone forth? He replies: 'I am capable of seeking that which has not been obtained; having obtained it, I preserve it so that it may not perish; and I am capable of acquiring again that which I have enjoyed, if I desire excellence. I am also capable of obtaining even that. If that is so, why have you gone forth? For by these four modes of worldly activity—the acquisition of sense objects and livelihoods—another person is harmed."

"If I am not a perpetrator of violence, this livelihood cannot be accomplished. If I am a farmer, I must cut down trees; if a warrior, then I must kill people; if a thief of others' wealth, then I must slay others; or if a merchant, I must speak falsehood with my own voice. Thus, all these evils arise in the world together with sense-objects. Having recognized this evil, I desire to go forth into the homeless life. Even for this ninth [type of person], there is no liberation."

Due to agitation regarding external objects and a lack of practice in the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), it is said that there are first four internal contentments and then five external ones, making nine contentments in total. For these nine contentments, the Great Sage established nine names. Because they cleanse the impurities of the objects of sense, these nine contentments are called by the name "water" (*salila*). They are: Ambhas, Salila, Ogha, Vṛṣṭi, Tāra, Sutāra, Sunetra, Sumarīca, and Uttamāmbhasika.
The nine powers contrary to these nine forms of dissatisfaction are declared to be those beginning with *anambhaḥ* and ending with *anuttamāmbhasika*. || 50 ||

The opponent says: "These three factors are incompatible with success (*siddhi*). Which factor is designated as 'success'? The Noble One answers with the following verse: "Reasoning, verbal testimony, study, the three-fold destruction of suffering, acquisition of friends, and charity—these are the eight successes. The former [three] are the three-fold goad of success. (51)

Inference, hearing, study... [and] the eight perfections resulting from giving. By means of these eightfold powers, the six destinies are accomplished. For example, a certain Brahmin who has gone forth and is studying the path reflects as follows: "What is the supreme livelihood? What is the truth? What is the ultimate goal? By doing what does knowledge arise, and does one obtain the perfection of illumination? When he has thus performed inference, he obtains knowledge.

"Pradhāna is distinct, buddhi is distinct, ahaṅkāra is distinct, the five tanmātras are distinct, the eleven indriyas are distinct, the five mahābhūtas are distinct, and the Paramātman is distinct. He observes defects in the five mahābhūtas; having seen the defects, agitation arises, and he then abandons the five mahābhūtas. This is called the "stage of delusion" (ūhapada). He observes defects in the eleven indriyas; having seen the defects, agitation arises.

Then one abandons the eleven organs; this is called the "Stage of Steadfastness" (*dhṛtipada*). Through the application of this knowledge, one perceives the defects in the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*). Having seen the defects, agitation arises; then one abandons the subtle elements. This is called the "Stage of Attainment" (*upagatasamapada*). One perceives the defects in the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) and the eightfold sovereign powers (*aiśvarya*). Having seen the defects, agitation arises; then one abandons the ego-sense and so forth. This is called the "Stage of Acquisition" (*prāptipada*).

One perceives a defect in *buddhi*. Having seen the defect, a sense of revulsion arises, and one attains the renunciation of *buddhi*. This is designated as the "state of cessation" (*nivṛtti-pada*). One perceives a defect in *pradhāna*. Having seen the defect, a sense of revulsion arises, and then one abandons *pradhāna*. This is called the "state of isolation" (*kaivalya-pada*). That Brahmin attains liberation through this process of reasoning (*ūha*). Because this perfection is attained through reasoning, it is designated as "perfection through reasoning" (*ūha-siddhi*). Thus, perfection through reasoning has been explained.

Now, the accomplishment through hearing (*śravaṇasiddhi*) is described. For example, suppose a certain Brāhmaṇa hears another person reciting the sound [of the Vedas]. [He understands: "That which is primary is distinct, the intellect is distinct, and so on up to the Supreme Self is distinct. Hearing this sound of recitation, he has understood the twenty-five categories (*tattva*). Then, having entered the stage of *ūha*, he abandons the five gross elements (*pañcabhūta*). Having entered the stage of *dhṛti*, he abandons the eleven organs (*indriya*).

Having entered the stage of *upagata*, one abandons the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*). Having entered the stage of *prāpti*, one abandons egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) and the rest. Having entered the stage of *nivṛtti*, one abandons the intellect (*buddhi*). Having entered the stage of *kaivalya*, one abandons primordial matter (*pradhāna*). This is designated as liberation (*mokṣa*). The perfection of hearing (*śravaṇa-siddhi*) has been explained. Now follows the perfection of study (*adhyayana-siddhi*). There are eight limbs of the intellect that bring about perfection. For example, a certain Brahmin goes to the teacher’s household (*gurukula*).

With affection, one serves; with faith, one hears the truth; one grasps it; having remembered it, one retains it; one understands the meanings of the words; one reflects; one discards misconceptions; and one penetrates things as they truly are. These are called the eight limbs of intelligence (*buddhyaṅga*). By means of these limbs of intelligence, one perceives the twenty-five principles (*tattva*); having entered the six realms of existence, one attains liberation. [Now follows] the accomplishment of the three-fold destruction of suffering: the destruction of internal suffering.

Just as a certain Brahmin, afflicted by internal suffering such as a disease of the head, goes to a physician and attains the alleviation of that illness; through this internal suffering, a desire to know arises. For the sake of seeking the knowledge of the cessation of the causes of this suffering, he goes to the family of a perfected guru. He applies himself to the eight limbs of wisdom (*buddhyaṅga*). He perceives the twenty-five principles (*tattva*). Through entering the contemplation of the six realms of existence, he attains liberation.

This accomplishment arises through internal suffering. Just as there is bodily suffering, so too is there mental suffering. There is also the warding off of external suffering. For example, a certain Brahmin might be afflicted by external suffering—namely, the suffering caused by the assault of humans, animals, birds, and even trees, stones, and so forth. Being unable to endure that, he proceeds with the desire to investigate the cessation of the causes of suffering; he goes to the teacher’s household.
