One practices the eight limbs of intelligence (*buddhyaṅga*). One perceives the twenty-five principles (*tattva*). Through entering the contemplation of the six destinies, one attains liberation. This accomplishment is obtained through external suffering; it is the warding off of superhuman (*ādhidaivika*) suffering. For example, suppose a certain Brahmin is afflicted by superhuman suffering such as cold, heat, rain, and so forth. Being unable to endure that, he approaches a teacher and requests the eight limbs of intelligence. He then perceives the twenty-five principles.

He enters into the observations of the six destinies; from this, he attains liberation. Regarding "attaining a spiritual friend": through the eight factors of enlightenment, one who has not yet attained knowledge obtains that which is exclusively beneficial from a *kalyāṇamitra* (spiritual friend). Once ultimate knowledge is attained, one attains liberation. This is the accomplishment of the cause of giving. For example, a certain Brahmin, hated by people, knows that another person hates him; therefore, he goes forth into homelessness (*pravrajati*). Once he has gone forth, even his teacher and fellow students hate him and do not grant him knowledge.

Realizing for himself his own lack of fortune, he goes to the edge of a village to live there. He says to himself, "This region is devoid of brahmins; here I shall dwell for the rainy season retreat. Having gone and stayed there, he receives much alms-food. He distributes the remainder among his friends, kinsmen, and even down to the cowherds and women of the village. Consequently, all the people in this village become affectionate toward him.

All people, desiring to provide for his residence during the rainy season retreat (*varṣāvāsa*), give him a triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*), a water vessel (*amatra*), robes, and other items. Then, when the festival of Indra (*śakrotsava*) is near, he says to the people: "Who will come with me to my great kingdom to see this festival? If you wish to go, all you people, having given me whatever you can, depart. Having gone there, he proceeds to the teacher's household (*gurukula*).

Having extracted the most excellent substance, one honors the teacher; the remainder is distributed in due order among fellow students. Then the teacher, friends, and all others become affectionate. At that time, the guru imparts knowledge. Through this knowledge, one attains ultimate knowledge; then one obtains liberation. This is the accomplishment (siddhi) obtained through knowledge. Regarding these eight accomplishments, other names have been established by the ancient great seers (maharṣis).

Svatārasiddhi (the accomplishment of self-delight), Sutārasiddhi (the accomplishment of son-delight), Tāratārasiddhi (the accomplishment of crossing-over-delight), Pramodatārasiddhi (the accomplishment of joy-delight), Pramuditatārasiddhi (the accomplishment of exultant-delight), Mohanatārasiddhi (the accomplishment of enchantment-delight), Ramyakatārasiddhi (the accomplishment of loveliness-delight), and Sadāpramuditatārasiddhi (the accomplishment of ever-exultant-delight). If these eight accomplishments are reversed, they are called the powers (*śaktis*), namely: Atārāśakti (the power of non-crossing) up to Asadāpramuditāśakti (the power of non-ever-exultant).

Thus, there are twenty-eight powers of incapacity (*aśakti*), consisting of the eleven powers of the impairment of the organs and the seventeen powers of the impairment of the intellect. These fifty categories, comprising the divisions of error (*viparyaya*), incapacity, contentment (*tuṣṭi*), and attainment (*siddhi*), have been described. The first three [categories] are the "restraints" (*aṅkuśa*) of attainment; just as an elephant in rut, when restrained by a goad, does not attain the independence it desires.

Thus, the world, constrained by the five misconceptions (*viparyaya*), the twenty-eight incapacities (*aśakti*), and the nine contentments (*tuṣṭi*), does not attain knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). If it abandons the knowledge of reality, then the eight perfections (*siddhi*) do not arise. Therefore, it has been said that the first three [categories] are the "restraints" (*aṅkuśa*) of perfection. Consequently, having abandoned misconceptions, incapacities, and contentments, one should practice until the eightfold perfections are attained. (51)

The opponent says: "The *liṅga* (subtle body) is permeated by the *bhāvas* (dispositions); therefore it transmigrates in *saṃsāra*," as was stated previously. The *liṅga* is of two kinds: the subtle *liṅga*, which arises at the beginning; and the body born of mother and father, along with the eleven organs. Both, joined together and permeated by the eight *bhāvas*, therefore transmigrate in *saṃsāra*. Here a doubt arises: what is produced first? Is the *liṅga* first, or are the *bhāvas* first? He states the answer in an *āryā* verse:
"There is no *liṅga* without the *bhāvas*, nor is there the manifestation of the *bhāvas* without the *liṅga*."
From that, creation is twofold: that which is called the Linga and that which is called Bhāva.

"Without entities (*bhāva*), the mark (*liṅga*) is not differentiated. If entities do not exist, the mark cannot be established, just as fire is not established without heat. "Without the subtle mark, there are no entities. If entities were devoid of a mark, they would not be established, just as heat is not established without fire. These two properties are mutually dependent, like fire and heat; and these two properties arise simultaneously, like the two horns of a cow.

"The creation is twofold, known as the *liṅga* and the *bhāva*. Thus, there are two designations for the modification of primordial nature (*prakṛti-vikāra*): the creation known as the *liṅga* and the creation known as the *bhāva*. At the very beginning of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), this twofold nature was established. The opponent asks: "Does this creation consist of only these two types, or is there yet another designation for it? This is resolved as follows:

The ancient seers established other names for it: *svatāra*. This person is exceedingly self-reliant (*sva-ūha-tīkṣṇa*); having attained wisdom alone, he accomplishes liberation, not through the instruction of another. Therefore, they say it is the "attainment through self-reliance" (*svatāra-siddhi*). Because one attains it by means of oneself alone and not by another, it is called *svatāra*. That very thing is wisdom (*prajñā*). For wisdom, having liberated one from this world, leads one to the world beyond; therefore, they designate it as the "time of supreme exertion" (*parākrānta-kāla*).

For at that time, it is called liberation (*mokṣa*). Liberation itself is designated as "accomplishment" (*siddhi*). The cause is called "the crossing" (*tāra*), and the fruit is called "accomplishment. Because this accomplishment of the crossing is obtained through one's own effort (*svahena*), they call it "self-accomplishment of the crossing" (*svatārasiddhi*). Subsequently, the seven accomplishments of the crossing are non-different, differing only in name: namely, "well-crossing accomplishment" (*sutārasiddhi*). One who has attained wisdom through both oneself and another accomplishes liberation.

This person, whose faculties are fully developed but slightly inferior, is able to attain liberation by means of much self-interest acquired through the instruction of another; therefore, they designate this as "the attainment of *sutāra*. It is called "the attainment of *tāratāra*" because it is attained exclusively through the instruction of another, hence it is *tāra*. This person is even more inferior than the former, possessing fully developed faculties; this is "the attainment of *pramoditāra*. This person, afflicted by internal suffering such as a headache or other ailments, goes to the teacher.

He seeks medical treatment. He obtains an immediate cessation of internal suffering. This leads to a single kind of joy. Then he reflects: "This is merely a cessation, not an absolute cessation. When there is isolation (*kaivalya*), then indeed there is absolute cessation; through this knowledge, he approaches a teacher of Sāṃkhya. He trains in wisdom. He seeks the attainment of liberation. He attains supreme bliss.

From this attainment of both kinds of joy, there arises the designation "the accomplishment of the flavor of joy" (*pramuditatārasiddhi*). This person, afflicted by both internal and external types of suffering, goes to a physician and requests treatment for these two sufferings. For when there is the immediate pacification of these two sufferings, at that very moment, both kinds of joy arise.

Knowing that this is not an ultimate cessation, he requests the teacher in order to train for the accomplishment of the *tāra* (the Savior). From the attainment of accomplishment comes joy, and thus one assumes the state called "Joyful" (*pramuditā*). This is the accomplishment of the *tāra* as the Deluder. This person, overcome by these three types of suffering—the internal suffering such as diseases of the head, the external suffering such as swords and clubs, and the divine suffering such as wind, rain, cold, and heat—goes to the teacher and requests medical treatment. For that medical treatment is preeminent.

This is designated as "delusion. Knowing that this is not an absolute cessation, one approaches the teacher and, through the practice of training, attains the accomplishment of *tāra*. From this, it receives the name "the accomplishment of *tāra* through delusion," and "the accomplishment of *tāra* through delight. This person, through the compassion and affection of the teacher, learns that accomplishment of *tāra* and receives that designation from the teacher; it is called "the accomplishment of perpetual joy."

This man, though hated by all, accepts gifts of wealth and clothing; having given them, he becomes affectionate toward everyone, and all desire to bring him success. Therefore, they say this is the accomplishment of the essence of constant joy. Regarding the incapacities: there are eleven incapacities resulting from the impairment of the sense faculties, and seventeen incapacities resulting from the impairment of the intellect; thus, there are twenty-eight incapacities in total.

It is established that fifty [states] have been described in total, including the five misconceptions (*viparyaya*), the nine contentments (*tuṣṭi*), and the eight perfections (*siddhi*). The first three are the "hooks" (*aṅkuśa*) of perfection; these consist of the five misconceptions, the twenty-eight incapacities (*aśakti*), and the nine contentments. These [first] are the hooks for the final elephant of the eight perfections. The eightfold perfections are capable of accomplishing liberation, but they cannot do so when restrained by the threefold hook.

Just as an intoxicated elephant, though worthy of independence, does not attain freedom as it pleases when restrained by a goad, so too it is with the eight siddhis. The eight siddhis are necessarily attained through the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna). The knowledge of reality is not attained by means of the threefold goad; therefore, one must certainly first abandon the threefold [goad] and diligently practice for the final eight siddhis.

The opponent says: Now, first regarding the meaning of the preceding term, I shall subsequently ask about the sequence. It was stated previously that "the *liṅga* (the subtle body) is perfumed by the *bhāvas* (states/dispositions), and therefore it transmigrates in *saṃsāra*. The *bhāvas* are exactly eight, namely: four *dharmas* (virtues) and four *adharmas* (non-virtues). The four *dharmas* are: virtue (*dharma*), knowledge (*jñāna*), dispassion (*virāga*), and sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). The four *adharmas* are precisely the opposites of these four *dharmas*. These are designated as the "eight *bhāvas*."

That which is permeated by the first four *dharmas* attains the state of a deity; that which is permeated by the last four *adharmas* attains the two states of humans and animals. Regarding the term "liṅga" as it is permeated, there are two kinds of *liṅgas*: the primary intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*) are called the subtle *liṅga*; that which has arisen from the five subtle elements and is joined with the eleven organs is called the gross *liṅga*.

Regarding these eight types of states and the two imbued characteristics (*adhivāsita-liṅga*), which arises first? Do the eight states arise first, or do the two characteristics arise first? This is resolved as follows: there are two explanations here. There is no temporal sequence of priority and posteriority between the eight states and the characteristic; they necessarily arise conjoined and simultaneously. Just as fire and heat do not exist apart from one another, or as the two horns of a cow necessarily manifest together at the same time.

Likewise, there are eight states and the subtle body (*liṅga*). When the subtle body—consisting of the primary matter (*pradhāna*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*)—exists, then necessarily among the eight states, the fourfold [qualities] exist. If the four qualities (*dharma*) do not exist, then the four [opposites, the] non-qualities (*adharma*) exist. Thus, both quality and non-quality are invariably inseparable from the subtle body. Likewise, even the gross body born of mother and father [is inseparable]; in this way, the subtle body also is invariably inseparable from the eight states.

There is a third creation called the elemental (bhautika). As Āryā has said: "The divine creation is of eight kinds, the animal creation is fivefold, and the human is of one kind; such, in brief, is the elemental creation. (53)

The divine course (*daivagati*) consists of eight varieties: the Brahma creation, the Prajāpati creation, the Indra creation, the Gandharva creation, the Asura creation, the Yakṣa creation, the Rākṣasa creation, and the Piśāca creation. The animal course (*tairyaggati*) consists of five varieties: the four-footed creation, the winged creation, the serpent creation, the general animal creation, and the stationary creation. The human course (*mānuṣyakagati*) consists of only one creation, because the human course comprises only a single genus.
The elemental [body] is said to be threefold; namely, the three consisting of the states of the characteristics of gods, animals, and humans. || 53 ||
The opponent asks: "Among the three worlds, where and what is perceived as predominant? He provides the answer in an Āryā verse:
"The creation is vast in *sattva* at the top and vast in *tamas* at the root;
in the middle, it is vast in *rajas*, extending from Brahmā down to a blade of grass. (54)

"Upwards, the realm of *sattva* is vast. In the abodes of the Brahma-creation and above, *sattva* is exceedingly vast; yet even here, *rajas* and *tamas* exist, though they are overwhelmed by *sattva*. Therefore, the gods, beginning with Brahmā, experience great bliss. "From the root, the creation is vast in *tamas*. This refers to the creation extending from animals and birds down to the stationary beings such as plants. Here, *tamas* is vast; yet even here, *rajas* and *sattva* exist, though they are overwhelmed by *tamas*. Therefore, animals and the like abound in delusion. "The creation from the root... [is thus described].

Among those three creations, because they—namely the animals and so forth—are the most inferior from the very root, it is said to be "from the base. Regarding the intermediate creation, it is said that "rajas predominates": in the human creation, rajas is predominant; yet both *sattva* and *tamas* are also present. Because of the abundance of *rajas* and because *sattva* and *tamas* are overwhelmed by it, sorrow and suffering are abundant among humans. The human state of existence is called "intermediate" because it occupies the middle position among the three states of existence. How is the final creation called "stump" (*stamba*)?

That which consists of herbs, trees, mountains, stones, and so forth, is called the "stambha" (the pillar) because the three worlds are supported by these. Thus, the creation of the subtle body (*liṅgasarga*), the creation of dispositions (*bhāvasarga*), and the material creation (*bhautikasarga*) have been described in every respect. This threefold creation is produced by *pradhāna*; therefore, the function of *pradhāna* is concluded. That is to say, having created the world, [the soul] attains liberation. 54.

An opponent asks: Among the three worlds—humans, gods, and animals—who experiences pleasure and pain? Is it *pradhāna* that experiences them, or do the intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), and so on up to the eleven organs experience them, or does this *puruṣa* experience them? The answer is given in verse: "In this world, the conscious *puruṣa* undergoes the suffering caused by old age and death;
because the *liṅga* (the subtle body) has not ceased [to function], therefore, in brief, there is suffering. (55)

In this regard, the conscious *puruṣa* alone undergoes the suffering of old age and death. In the three worlds, there exists the suffering caused by old age: wrinkled skin, graying hair, shortness of breath, the need for a staff for support, being treated with contempt by kinsmen and friends—all such sufferings have old age as their cause. As for the "suffering of death": it is like a man who, having attained desired sovereignty, or perhaps one who perceives the five subtle objects of sense.

Or, if one perceives gross objects, having approached death, one is seized by Yama; herein one experiences the suffering known as the suffering of death. Furthermore, there are three intermediate sufferings which a conscious person (*puruṣa*) experiences. Primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and the gross body do not experience them, because they are insentient. Therefore it is said that suffering belongs to the *puruṣa*, and not to primordial matter and the rest. The opponent says:

For how long does the *puruṣa* experience these sufferings? The answer is given: "As long as the *liṅga* has not ceased, therefore this is summarized as 'suffering. When the *liṅga*, beginning with the *mahat*, which constitutes the suffering of the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*), does not cease—meaning when this gross body (*sthūla-śarīra*) transmigrates in the world and does not cease—during such a period the *puruṣa* experiences suffering. When the subtle and gross *liṅga* ceases, then the *puruṣa* is liberated. When he is liberated...

At that time, one does not experience such sufferings to the ultimate degree. When neither the subtle nor the gross *liṅga* (body) has ceased, then the *puruṣa* does not attain liberation from suffering. Therefore, it has been stated in brief that both the subtle *liṅga* and the gross *liṅga* are suffering. || 55 ||
